Jehoshaphat was in trouble. He had just heard the news that a great multitude was coming to fight against him. At that moment he did what all of us naturally do when a multitude of problems come against us. He was afraid. How well I know the feeling of fear, the dread that grips my heart at times. Sometimes it’s the big things, like being misunderstood and misused, or the fear and pain of sickness, or the death of a loved one. Sometimes it’s small things, like loneliness on a Sunday afternoon. This is not comfortable, God, and I’m afraid.

Jehoshaphat laid his fear aside, set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all the land of Judah – verse 3. Even in this seemingly impossible situation of having thousands of men on their way to destroy him and his people, he fell before the Lord and acknowledged His perfect, omnipotent rule. And [he] said, O LORD God of our fathers, art not thou God in heaven? and rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen? and in thine hand is there not power and might, so that none is able to withstand thee? –verse 6.

The choice is mine. I wrestle with my own fearful thoughts, turning them over and over in my mind as if hoping to change the situation with my messy and fearful concoctions. Clinging to my fear gives me a feeling of being in control. But it is killing me from the inside out, even without the dreaded “what ifs” becoming reality. Finally, I let go and fall exhausted at my Lord’s feet, and my heart echoes the words of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah.

In humble entreaty, Jehoshaphat acknowledges their weakness and need for God’s power. O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. –verse 12.

Yes, God, I am nothing in the grand scheme of things. I have no power, not even to be the fruitful worker in Your kingdom that I always dreamed of being. I can’t fight this battle.

Jehoshaphat realized that he alone, as one man, had no strength. He called all the people of Judah together, And all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children –verse 13. They knew the strength in unity. As they stood before the Lord, waiting for Him to speak, the Spirit of the Lord came down and God gave them the words of help and hope that they were desperate for.

…Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s –verse 15. Often I try to fight my battles inside of myself rather than making myself vulnerable to others. But, as soon as I invite others into my life and into my battles, I find the strength of God through His people. When we are confused and disillusioned, we need the people of God. When we all pray together, we will get an answer to our prayer for direction.

Jehoshaphat heard the next directive from God. Tomorrow go ye down against them … Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD … fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you –verses 16-17. These words comfort my heart. Often the easiest thing to do is try to fix things, to quickly come up with a remedy of some sort to get myself out of this dilemma, to try to convince myself that everything will be okay. But God tells my heart to sit still without fear and let Him do the fighting. This takes more spiritual muscle than all the action, all the doing, and all the worrying; plus, it accomplishes a lot more.

And Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshipping the LORD –verse 18. If I obey and trust instead of worry and sit still instead of jumping into the middle of things, then I will see God do miracles. No, not always in changing my circumstances or removing all the hard things, but He does a miracle in my own soul which changes my focus and attitude. And that causes me to worship because it’s a miracle which only the all-mighty, all-powerful God can do.

Do you think any of them slept that night? They knew a fearsome army was on its way to destroy them and yet… they had heard God speak. Just perhaps there was a joyful expectation in their hearts and an eager anticipation to see how God was going to win this battle. When I learn to practice trust in the little things and the big things that pile into my life, I will soon learn to have a heart of excited expectation, because I know He is going to do something! He is going to give me a way out. Even if the worst happens, He will show my heart the way of peace and He has promised to be with me through it all. And after all, the ultimate victory is already won, so what do all these infractions really have to do with my peace and joy? Nothing.

Morning dawned; it was the day God had told them to go out against these enemies. They arose with no delay. They all knew obedience was paramount in receiving God’s blessing that day. And as they went out of the city, Jehoshaphat exhorted them. And they rose early in the morning, …and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, …Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper. And… he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army… – verses 21-20. He appointed singers to sing as they went, proclaiming to everyone and to the opposing army that they were on the Lord’s side.

I would have liked to see that huge army going out of the city, singing. They were facing a daunting task and one that would have made the strongest man tremble, but they were singing. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set… [an ambush] against the children of Ammon, [and] Moab, …which were come against Judah; and they were smitten …every one helped to destroy another –verses 22-23.

The people of Judah went to their watch tower and in amazement saw that their enemies had destroyed each other, and they saw nothing but an army of dead bodies. When a fearsome battle is set in array against me, I can still make the decision to trust and sing. Singing is a deliberate act of worship; it reminds our own souls and the souls of everyone listening that the Lord, He is God. He is the One in complete charge of my circumstances, of my tiny world, and all its problems. Suddenly the enemies are dead. The circumstances may not have changed, but the battle is finished in my soul.

The army of Judah spent the next three days gathering the riches and spoils from the dead bodies of their enemies, collecting so much that they couldn’t carry it all away with them. Astonishing! But that is how it is every time. My spirit benefits from the hard things that I endure successfully. Each victory allows me to collect ‘spoils’ which will profit me for the rest of my life. My heart is full of blessing, of being cared for, and being carried by a Heavenly Father. The “armies of Moab and Ammon” have brought blessing instead of ruin.

They came again to their homes in Jerusalem with singing, and harps, and trumpets, overloaded with all their spoil. The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of the land when they heard how God had fought this huge battle, then Jehoshaphat’s realm was quiet. Peace reigned.

The peace of knowing that all I really need is God and His working in my life is the ultimate peace. This broken world can bring all manner of pain, sickness, and disappointments, but God brings rest to the heart that was once so full of tumult and fear. There is rest ‘round about’ and all the ‘kingdoms of the land’ will be amazed and curious at the strength that is within us, because it is the strength that no one can match—the strength of our amazing God.

Jéhosaphat était en difficulté. Il venait d’apprendre la nouvelle qu’une grande multitude venait pour combattre contre lui. À cet instant, il fit ce que nous faisons tous naturellement lorsque des flots de problèmes se présentent à nous. Il eut peur. Comme je connais bien ce sentiment de peur, cette angoisse qui serre parfois mon cœur. Parfois ce sont les choses importantes, comme être incompris et mal utilisé, ou la peur et la douleur de la maladie, ou la mort d’un être cher. Parfois ce sont des choses petites, comme la solitude un dimanche après‑midi. Cela n’est pas confortable, Seigneur, et j’ai peur.

Jéhosaphat mit sa peur de côté, se mit à chercher le Seigneur et proclama un jeûne dans tout le pays de Juda – verset 3. Même dans cette situation apparemment impossible où des milliers d’hommes étaient en route pour le détruire lui et son peuple, il tomba devant le Seigneur et reconnut Son règne parfait et omnipotent. Et [il] dit: Seigneur Dieu de nos pères, n’es‑tu pas Dieu dans les cieux? et ne gouvernes‑tu pas tous les royaumes des païens? et n’est‑il pas dans ta main le pouvoir et la force, de sorte que nul ne peut te résister? – verset 6.

Le choix m’appartient. Je lutte avec mes propres pensées craintives, les retournant encore et encore dans mon esprit comme si j’espérais changer la situation avec mes mixtures confuses et peureuses. M’accrocher à ma peur me donne l’illusion du contrôle. Mais cela me tue de l’intérieur, même sans que les redoutés “et si” deviennent réalité. Finalement, je lâche prise et tombe, épuisée, aux pieds de mon Seigneur, et mon cœur fait écho aux paroles de Jéhosaphat, le roi de Juda.

Dans une humble supplication, Jéhosaphat reconnaît leur faiblesse et leur besoin de la puissance de Dieu. Ô notre Dieu, ne jugeras‑tu pas d’eux? car nous n’avons point de force contre cette grande compagnie qui vient contre nous; nous ne savons que faire: mais nos yeux sont sur toi. – verset 12.

Oui, Dieu, je ne suis rien dans l’ensemble des choses. Je n’ai aucun pouvoir, pas même pour être l’ouvrière féconde dans Ton royaume dont j’ai toujours rêvé. Je ne peux pas mener ce combat.

Jéhosaphat comprit qu’il était seul, comme un homme, sans force. Il rassembla tout le peuple de Juda, Et tout Juda se tint devant l’Éternel, avec leurs petits, leurs femmes, et leurs enfants – verset 13. Ils connaissaient la force de l’unité. Tandis qu’ils se tenaient devant le Seigneur, attendant qu’Il parle, l’Esprit de l’Éternel descendit et Dieu leur donna les paroles d’aide et d’espérance dont ils étaient si désespérément avides.

…N’ayez point peur et ne soyez point effrayés à cause de cette grande multitude; car la bataille n’est pas la vôtre, mais celle de Dieu – verset 15. Souvent j’essaie de mener mes batailles à l’intérieur de moi au lieu de me rendre vulnérable devant d’autres. Mais, dès que j’invite d’autres personnes dans ma vie et dans mes combats, je trouve la force de Dieu à travers son peuple. Quand nous sommes confus et désillusionnés, nous avons besoin du peuple de Dieu. Quand nous prions tous ensemble, nous recevrons une réponse à notre prière pour la direction.

Jéhosaphat entendit la directive suivante de Dieu. Demain, descendez contre eux … Vous n’aurez point besoin de combattre en cette bataille: placez‑vous, tenez‑vous tranquilles, et voyez la délivrance de l’Éternel … ne craignez point, et ne soyez point effrayés; demain sortez contre eux: car l’Éternel sera avec vous – versets 16‑17. Ces paroles consolent mon cœur. Souvent la chose la plus facile est d’essayer de réparer les choses, de trouver vite un remède quelconque pour me sortir de ce dilemme, d’essayer de me convaincre que tout ira bien. Mais Dieu dit à mon cœur de rester tranquille sans peur et de lui laisser faire la lutte. Cela demande plus de muscles spirituels que toute l’action, tout le faire et tout l’inquiéter; de plus, cela accomplit bien davantage.

Et Jéhosaphat baissa sa tête, face contre terre: et tout Juda et les habitants de Jérusalem tombèrent devant l’Éternel, et adorèrent l’Éternel – verset 18. Si j’obéis et que je fais confiance au lieu de m’inquiéter, et que je reste immobile au lieu de me jeter au milieu des choses, alors je verrai Dieu opérer des miracles. Non, pas toujours en changeant mes circonstances ou en retirant toutes les épreuves, mais Il fait un miracle dans mon âme qui change mon regard et mon attitude. Et cela me conduit à adorer parce que c’est un miracle que seul l’Éternel tout‑puissant peut accomplir.

Pensez‑vous qu’ils aient pu dormir cette nuit‑là? Ils savaient qu’une armée redoutable venait pour les détruire et pourtant… ils avaient entendu Dieu parler. Peut‑être y avait‑il une attente joyeuse dans leurs cœurs et une anticipation impatiente de voir comment Dieu allait gagner cette bataille. Quand j’apprends à pratiquer la confiance dans les petites choses et les grandes choses qui s’accumulent dans ma vie, j’apprendrai bientôt à avoir un cœur d’attente joyeuse, car je sais qu’Il va agir! Il va me donner une issue. Même si le pire arrive, Il montrera à mon cœur la voie de la paix et Il a promis d’être avec moi à travers tout cela. Et après tout, la victoire ultime est déjà gagnée, alors en quoi toutes ces atteintes affectent‑elles vraiment ma paix et ma joie? Rien.

Le matin se leva; c’était le jour où Dieu leur avait dit de sortir contre ces ennemis. Ils se levèrent sans délai. Ils savaient tous que l’obéissance était primordiale pour recevoir la bénédiction de Dieu ce jour‑là. Et lorsqu’ils sortirent de la ville, Jéhosaphat les exhorta. Et ils se levèrent de bon matin, …et comme ils partaient, Jéhosaphat se tint debout et dit, …Croyez en l’Éternel votre Dieu, et vous serez affermis; croyez ses prophètes, et vous prospérerez. Et… il nomma des chantres pour l’Éternel, qui devaient louer la beauté de la sainteté, pendant qu’ils marchaient devant l’armée… – versets 21‑20. Il désigna des chantres pour chanter en sortant, proclamant à tous et à l’armée ennemie qu’ils étaient du côté du Seigneur.

J’aurais aimé voir cette énorme armée sortir de la ville en chantant. Ils faisaient face à une tâche intimidante qui aurait fait trembler l’homme le plus robuste, mais ils chantaient. Et quand ils commencèrent à chanter et à louer, l’Éternel plaça… [une embuscade] contre les enfants d’Ammon, et de Moab, …qui étaient venus contre Juda; et ils furent frappés … chacun aidait à détruire l’autre – versets 22‑23.

Le peuple de Juda alla à leur tour de garde et constata, dans l’étonnement, que leurs ennemis s’étaient détruits les uns les autres, et ils ne virent rien d’autre qu’une armée de cadavres. Quand une bataille redoutable est dressée contre moi, je peux encore décider de faire confiance et de chanter. Le chant est un acte délibéré d’adoration; il rappelle à notre propre âme et aux âmes de tous ceux qui écoutent que le Seigneur, c’est Lui le Dieu. Il est Celui qui a le contrôle total de mes circonstances, de mon petit monde, et de tous ses problèmes. Soudain, les ennemis sont morts. Les circonstances n’ont peut‑être pas changé, mais la bataille est finie dans mon âme.

L’armée de Juda passa les trois jours suivants à rassembler les richesses et les dépouilles des corps de leurs ennemis, amassant tellement qu’ils ne purent tout emporter. Étonnant! Mais c’est toujours ainsi. Mon esprit bénéficie des choses difficiles que je surmonte avec succès. Chaque victoire me permet de recueillir des « dépouilles » qui me profiteront pour le reste de ma vie. Mon cœur est rempli de bénédiction, de soins et d’être porté par un Père céleste. Les « armées de Moab et d’Ammon » ont apporté la bénédiction au lieu de la ruine.

Ils revinrent chez eux à Jérusalem en chantant, avec harpes et trompettes, surchargés de toutes leurs dépouilles. La crainte de Dieu tomba sur tous les royaumes du pays quand ils entendirent comment Dieu avait combattu cette grande bataille, puis le royaume de Jéhosaphat fut tranquille. La paix régna.

La paix de savoir que tout ce dont j’ai vraiment besoin, c’est Dieu et Son action dans ma vie, est la paix ultime. Ce monde brisé peut apporter toutes sortes de douleur, de maladie et de déceptions, mais Dieu apporte le repos au cœur qui était autrefois si plein de tumulte et de peur. This hymn is generally thought to be one of the most loved hymns written during the latter part of the 19th century. The writing of this thoughtful and beautifully constructed text is even more amazing when we consider that its author was one who was almost completely blind and who describes the writing of this hymn as the “fruit of much mental suffering,” and “the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life.”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, March 27, 1842, George Matheson had only partial vision as a boy, and, after entering Glasgow University, his eyesight continued to fail rapidly. Except for “moments of shadowy eyesight”, he was totally blind by the age of 18. This affliction of blindness seemed to be a tragedy since he was an eager and avid scholar, yet it caused him to trust in the Lord, and it strengthened his walk with God.

He entered the university at the early age of 15 and graduated with high honors in 1861 at the age of 19. He was a brilliant scholar, even spending four more years after graduation in more theological studies, all the while remaining single. After his graduation he became entirely dependent on others, relying much upon his two sisters, who were so dedicated that they learned Latin, Greek, and Hebrew since they thought it might aid him in his theological studies. One of them continued to be his faithful co-worker and helper throughout his life, assisting in his calling of being a pastor and other ministerial duties.

After completing his theological course, he became assistant pastor to the renowned Dr. Macduff, in whose church of thousands of members he had been brought up. Soon, however, he was chosen minister of the Church of Scotland in the seaport summer resort of Innellan. Here he stayed for eighteen years. Many families came to spend the summer there chiefly to be inspired by his preaching ministry.

Whenever he preached, the open Bible was before him as he stood in the pulpit, and to the congregation, he seemed to be reading from it. During the messages, his eyes looked straight at the congregation, and many went away with no clue that they just listened to a blind preacher. It was during this time that he made a practice of memorizing his sermons, as well as the passages of Scripture he used in his messages. His memory was so sharp that if someone read one of his prepared sermons to him twice, or whatever else he wanted to memorize, he could from then on repeat it perfectly. One Sunday, however, after doing this for 12 years, when in the middle of a powerful sermon his memory completely collapsed, and the topic on which he was preaching vanished from his mind. He sat down and commenced to request a psalm to be sung, and, after the song, with perfect calmness told the audience what had happened. With this done, he stood to his feet, gave out a new text, and preached an impromptu sermon of great power. After that experience George wrote little of his sermons, and finally prepared only an outline from which to preach.

Dr. Matheson’s final pastorate was taken up in 1886 at the age of 44 where he became pastor of the large St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, where his eloquent preaching consistently attracted large throngs of people to the services. Here he remained for 13 years, his church growing from 1,494 members to 1,703 in the first 5 years. He continued faithfully preaching the gospel and became well known as one of Scotland’s outstanding preachers and pastors and was greatly esteemed in Edinburgh where he resided.

Many speculations have been made regarding the cause of the mental distress which prompted the author to write this text. A very popular account, although never verified, is that this text was a result of the severe trial Matheson faced after his soon-to-be bride left him just before their marriage when she learned of his impending total blindness. Although this story cannot be documented, there are many significant hints in this hymn reflecting a saddened heart, such as the “flickering torch” and the “borrowed ray” in the second verse, the tracing of the “rainbow through the rain” in the third stanza, as well as the “cross” in the last verse.

Fortunately, Dr. Matheson did relate an account of his writing of this hymn:

“My hymn was composed in the manse of Innellan on the evening of June 6, 1882. I was at that time alone. It was the day of my sister’s wedding, and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow. Something happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering and was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. A genuine inspiration, I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes and equally sure it never received at my hands any retouching or correction. I have no natural gift of rhythm. All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

يُعتقد عمومًا أن هذه الأنشودة هي واحدة من أكثر الترانيم المحبوبة التي كُتبت خلال الجزء الأخير من القرن التاسع عشرth. إن كتابة هذا النص المتأمل والمبني بشكل جميل تزداد إدهاشًا إذا أخذنا بعين الاعتبار أن مؤلفه كان شبه أعمى تقريبًا ويصف كتابة هذه الأنشودة بأنها «ثمرة معاناة عقلية عظيمة»، و«أسرع قدر من العمل قمت به في حياتي».

وُلد في غلاسغو باسكتلندا في 27 مارس 1842، كان جورج ماثيسون يرى جزئيًا عندما كان صبيًا، وبعد التحاقه بجامعة غلاسغو استمرت بصره في التدهور بسرعة. باستثناء «لحظات من البصر الظلي»، كان أعمى تمامًا بحلول سن الثامنة عشرة. بدا هذا البلاء من العمى مأساةً بما أنه كان عالمًا نهمًا ومتحمسًا، ومع ذلك دفعه إلى الثقة بالرب، وقوّى سيره مع الله.

التحق بالجامعة في سن مبكرة بلغت 15 عامًا وتخرّج بامتياز في عام 1861 عن عمر يناهز 19 عامًا. كان عالمًا بارعًا، وقضى حتى أربع سنوات أخرى بعد التخرج في دراسات لاهوتية إضافية، وظل طوال ذلك الوقت أعزب. بعد تخرجه أصبح معتمدًا تمامًا على الآخرين، معتمدًا بشكل كبير على شقيقتيه اللتين كانتا مخلصتين لدرجة أنهما تعلّمتا اللاتينية واليونانية والعبرية لأنهما ظنّتا أن ذلك قد يساعده في دراساته اللاهوتية. واصلت إحداهما أن تكون زميلته المخلصة والمساعدة طوال حياته، مساعدًا في رسالته كراعٍ وواجباته الوزارية الأخرى.

بعد إتمام دراسته اللاهوتية، أصبح مساعدًا للواعظ الشهير الدكتور ماكدف، في كنيسة هذا الأخير التي نشأ فيها بين آلاف الأعضاء. لكن سرعان ما اختير وزيرًا لكنيسة أسكتلندا في منتجع البحر الصيفي إنيلان. مكث هناك ثمانية عشر عامًا. جاؤوا إلى هناك كثيرًا لقضاء الصيف بشكل رئيسي ليستنشقوا الإلهام من خدمته الوعظية.

كلما وعظ كان الكتاب المقدس المفتوح أمامه وهو واقف في المنبر، وللجماعة بدا كأنه يقرأ منه. خلال العظات كانت عيناه تنظران مباشرة إلى الجمهور، وذهب كثيرون دون أن يخلّف ذلك أي مؤشر على أنهم كانوا يستمعون لتوهم إلى واعظ أعمى. خلال هذه الفترة اعتاد أن يحفظ عظاته وكذلك المقاطع الكتابية التي يستخدمها في رسائله. كانت ذاكرته حادة جدًا بحيث إن قرأ له أحدهم إحدى عظاته المعدة مرتين، أو أي شيء آخر أراد أن يحفظه، فإنه من ذلك الحين كان يستطيع تكرارها تمامًا. لكن في أحد الأيام الأحد، وبعد أن فعل ذلك لمدة 12 عامًا، انهارت ذاكرته تمامًا في منتصف موعظة قوية، وتلاشى الموضوع الذي كان يوعظ عنه من ذهنه. جلس وطلب أن تُغنّى مزامير، وبعد النشيد أخبر الجمهور بهدوء تام بما حدث. وبعد أن فعل ذلك وقف، وطرح نصًا جديدًا، ووعظ موعظة مرتجلة ذات قوة كبيرة. بعد تلك الحادثة كتب جورج قليلًا من عظاته، وفي النهاية جهّز مخططًا فقط للاعتماد عليه في الوعظ.

تولّى الدكتور ماثيسون رعايته النهائية في عام 1886 عن عمر 44 عندما أصبح راعٍ لكنيسة سانت برنارد الكبيرة في إدنبرة، حيث كان وعظه البليغ يجذب باستمرار حشودًا كبيرة إلى الخدمات. مكث هناك 13 عامًا، ونمت الكنيسة من 1,494 عضوًا إلى 1,703 في السنوات الخمس الأولى. واصل بشغف تبشير الإنجيل وأصبح معروفًا كأحد أبرز الوعاظ والرعاة في اسكتلندا وكان محل تقدير كبير في إدنبرة حيث أقام.

ذُكرت تكهنات كثيرة حول سبب الضيق العقلي الذي دفع المؤلف إلى كتابة هذا النص. رواية شائعة جدًا، وإن لم تُثبَت أبدًا، هي أن هذا النص كان نتيجة المحنة الشديدة التي واجهها ماثيسون بعد أن تركته خطيبته التي توشك أن تتزوج به قبل زفافهما عندما علمت بأنه سيعمى تمامًا. ومع أن هذه القصة لا يمكن توثيقها، فهناك العديد من التلميحات المهمة في هذه الأنشودة التي تعكس قلبًا حزينًا، مثل «المشعل المتلألئ» و«الشعاع المستعار» في المقطع الثاني، ورصد «قوس قزح من خلال المطر» في المقطع الثالث، وكذلك «الصليب» في المقطع الأخير.

لحسن الحظ، رواى الدكتور ماثيسون قصة كتابة هذه الأنشودة:

«كُتبت أنشودتي في مسكن القسيس في إنيلان في مساء 6 يونيو 1882. كنت في ذلك الوقت وحيدًا. كان ذلك يوم زفاف أختي، وبقي بقية العائلة في غلاسغو طوال الليل. حدث لي شيء، لم يكن معروفًا إلا لي فقط، وقد سبب لي أعظم معاناة عقلية. كانت الأنشودة ثمرة تلك المعاناة وكانت أسرع قطعة عمل قمت بها في حياتي. كانت وحيًا حقيقيًا، كان لدي الانطباع أكثر أن أحد الأصوات الداخلية هو الذي همسها لي لا أنني كتبها بنفسي. أنا متأكد تمامًا أن العمل كله اكتمل في خمس دقائق ومتأكد بنفس القدر أنه لم يتلق عند يدي أي تعديل أو تصحيح. ليس لدي موهبة طبيعية في الإيقاع. كل الأبيات الأخرى التي كتبتها هي مقالات مصنعة؛ هذه أتت كفجر آتي من فوق. لم أتمكن أبدًا من استعادة نفس الحماس في الشعر.»

ظهرت الأنشودة أول مرة في مجلة كنيسة اسكتلندا الشهرية، Life and Work، في يناير 1883. وقد لُحن اللحن بعد عام واحد بواسطة عازف أورغان اسكتلندي بارز في زمانه، ألبرت إل. بيس، الذي طُلب منه أن يكتب لحنًا خصيصًا لنص ماثيسون.

وصف بيس نفسه كتابة هذا اللحن الجميل كما يلي: «بعد أن قرأته بعناية كتبت الموسيقى مباشرةً، ويمكنني القول إن حبر النغمة الأولى لم يكن قد جف تقريبًا عندما أنهيت اللحن.» أما أصل اسم اللحن، St. Margaret، فغير معروف باستثناء أنه اسم محترم جدًا في اسكتلندا، وبالتأكيد نسبة إلى الملكة المحبوبة مارجريت ملكة اسكتلندا.

قضى ماثيسون سنواته الأخيرة من عمره من سن 57 حتى وفاته عن عمر 64 في كتابة بعض أروع الكتابات التأملية باللغة الإنجليزية، بما في ذلك Moments on the Mount وVoice of the Spirit وRests by the River. وعلى الرغم من أن هذه هي أنشودته الوحيدة الموجودة في معظم كتب الترانيم، فقد كتب بعض الترانيم الجميلة الأخرى، بما في ذلك «Make Me A Captive Lord»، و«Then I Shall Be Free.»

الكلمات الأربع الأساسية في «O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go» هي: المحبة، والنور، والفرح، والصليب. وُصفت هذه الكلمات بأنها الإشباع الكامل لأي مؤمن حياته مستسلمة تمامًا لمشيئة الله. وقد يستغرق اكتشاف الدلالة الشخصية لهذه التعبيرات الأربع بقية حياة المرء.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

এই স্তবক সাধারণত 19th শতকের শেষভাগে রচিত সবচেয়ে প্রিয় স্তবকগুলোর একটি বলে বিবেচিত হয়। এই চিন্তাশীল ও সাবলীলভাবে নির্মিত লেখাটি লেখা আরও দৃশ্যমানভাবে আশ্চর্যজনক যখন আমরা বিবেচনা করি যে এর রচয়িতা ছিল এমন একজন যিনি প্রায় সম্পূর্ণ অন্ধ ছিলেন এবং যিনি এই স্তবক রচনা করা কে বর্ণনা করেছেন “অনেক মানসিক কষ্টের ফল,” এবং “আমি জীবনে যত দ্রুত কাজ করেছি তার মধ্যে এটি সবচেয়ে দ্রুত ছিল।”

জর্জ ম্যাথিসন গ্লাসগো, স্কটল্যান্ডে 27 মার্চ, 1842-এ জন্মগ্রহণ করেন; ছোটবেলায় তাঁর দৃষ্টি আংশিক ছিল, এবং গ্লাসগো বিশ্ববিদ্যালয়ে প্রবেশের পর তাঁর দৃষ্টি দ্রুত খারাপ হতে থাকে। “ছায়াময় দৃষ্টির মুহূর্ত” ছাড়া, 18 বছর বয়সে তিনি সম্পূর্ণ অন্ধ হয়ে যান। এই অন্ধত্বটি একটি ট্র্যাজেডির মতো মনে হতে পারে কারণ তিনি ছিলেন একজন উদ্দীপ্ত ও আগ্রহী পণ্ডিত, তবু এতে তাঁকে প্রভুর উপর বিশ্বাস স্থাপন করতে সাহায্য হল এবং এটি তাঁর ঈশ্বরের সঙ্গে চলায় শক্তি জোগালো।

তিনি মাত্র 15 বছর বয়সে বিশ্ববিদ্যালয়ে প্রবেশ করেছিলেন এবং 1861 সালে 19 বছর বয়সে উচ্চ সম্মানসহ স্নাতক হন। তিনি একজন উজ্জ্বল পণ্ডিত ছিলেন; স্নাতকের পরে তিনি আরও চার বছর ধর্মতাত্ত্বিক অধ্যয়নে সময় কাটালেন, সেই সময়ও তিনি অবিবাহিত ছিলেন। স্নাতকের পর তিনি সম্পূর্ণরূপে অন্যদের ওপর নির্ভরশীল হয়ে পড়েন, বিশেষ করে তাঁর দুই বোনের ওপর, যারা এতটাই নিবেদিত ছিল যে ল্যাটিন, গ্রিক ও হিব্রু শিখে নেন কারণ তারা ধারণা করেছিল এটি তাঁর ধর্মতাত্ত্বিক অধ্যয়নে সহায়ক হবে। তাঁদের একজন সারাজীবন ধরে তাঁর বিশ্বস্ত সহকর্মী ও সহায়ক ছিলেন, পাদরিত্ব ও অন্যান্য ধর্মসেবামূলক দায়িত্বে সহায়তা করেছিলেন।

থিওলজিক্যাল কোর্স শেষ করার পর তিনি বিশিষ্ট ড. ম্যাকডাফের সহকারী পাদরি হন, যাঁর বিশাল সদস্যসংখ্যার চার্চে তিনি বড় হয়েছিলেন। কিন্তু শীঘ্রই তাকে ইননেলান নামে সমুদ্রতীরবর্তী গ্রীষ্মকালীন রিসর্টে চার্চ অব স্কটল্যান্ডের মন্ত্রী নির্বাচিত করা হয়। এখানে তিনি আঠারো বছর কাটালেন। অনেক পরিবার গ্রীষ্মে সেখানে আসত, প্রধানত তাঁর প্রচার থেকে অনুপ্রাণিত হওয়ার জন্য।

যখনই তিনি খিতব দিতেন, খোলা বাইবেল তাঁর সামনে পিউলপিটে থাকত, এবং শ্রোতাদের কাছে তিনি যেন তাতে থেকে পড়ছেন—এমনই মনে হতো। বক্তৃতার সময় তাঁর চোখ সরাসরি শ্রোতাদের দিকে থাকত, এবং অনেকেই এই বিশ্বাস ছাড়াই বেরিয়ে যেত যে তারা আসলে একটি অন্ধ প্রচারককে শুনেছে। এই সময়েই তিনি তাঁর প্রবচনগুলো মুখস্ত রাখার অভ্যাস গড়ে তুলেছিলেন, এবং তিনি যা যা শাস্ত্রে উদ্ধৃত করতেন তা স্মৃতিতেই রাখতেন। তাঁর স্মৃতি এত তীক্ষ্ণ ছিল যে কেউ যদি তাঁর প্রস্তুতকৃত বক্তৃতার একটিকে তাঁকে দুইবার পড়ে শোনাত বা তিনি যা কিছুই মনে রাখতে চেয়েছিলেন—তাহলে এরপর থেকে তিনি তা নিখুঁতভাবে পুনরাবৃত্তি করতে পারতেন। এক রবিবার, তবু, দুই-বার এভাবে করবার বারো বছর পর, এক শক্তিশালী উপদেশের মাঝখানে তাঁর স্মৃতি সম্পূর্ণরূপে ভেঙে পড়ে এবং তিনি যে বিষয়টি প্রচার করছিলেন তা তাঁর মনে থেকে উধাও হয়ে যায়। তিনি বসে গিয়ে একটি স্তবক গাওয়ার অনুরোধ করলেন, এবং গান শেষে পুরো শান্তচিত্তে শ্রোতাদের জানালেন কী ঘটেছে। এরপর তিনি দাঁড়িয়ে একটি নতুন পাঠ ঘোষণা করলেন এবং একটি আকস্মিক কিন্তু অত্যন্ত শক্তিশালী উপদেশ দিলেন। সেই অভিজ্ঞতার পরে জর্জ খুব কমই তাঁর উপদেশ লিখতেন, এবং অবশেষে শুধু একটি রূপরেখা তৈরি করতেন যেখান থেকে তিনি প্রচার করতেন।

ড. ম্যাথিসনের শেষ পাদরিত্ব 1886 সালে শুরু হয় যখন তিনি 44 বছর বয়সে এডিনবার্গের বড় সেন্ট বার্নার্ডস প্যারিশ চার্চের পাদরি হন, যেখানে তাঁর বাগাড়ম্বর প্রচার নিয়মিতভাবে অনেকে কে সেবায় আকৃষ্ট করত। এখানে তিনি 13 বছর কাটালেন; প্রথম 5 বছরে তাঁর চার্চের সদস্যসংখ্যা 1,494 থেকে বেড়ে 1,703 হয়। তিনি বিশ্বস্তভাবে সুসমাচার প্রচার চালিয়ে গেলেন এবং স্কটল্যান্ডের একজন বিশিষ্ট প্রচারক ও পাদরিরূপে সুপরিচিত হন এবং এডিনবার্গে যেখানে তিনি বসবাস করতেন সেখানে তাঁকে ব্যাপক সম্মান দেওয়া হত।

রচয়িতাকে যে মানসিক কষ্টটি এই পাঠ রচনায় অনুপ্রাণিত করেছিল তার কারণ সম্পর্কে অনেক গোষ্ঠীভিত্তিক অনুমান আছে। একটি অত্যন্ত জনপ্রিয় বিবরণ—যদি না কখনো প্রমাণিত—হল যে এই পাঠটি ছিল ম্যাথিসনের সম্মুখীন হওয়া কঠোর পরীক্ষার ফল, যখন তাঁর সহধর্মিণী হতে যাওয়া ব্যক্তি বিবাহের ঠিক আগে তাঁকে ছেড়ে চলে গেলে, কারণ সে তাঁর আসন্ন সম্পূর্ণ অন্ধত্ব জানতে পেয়েছিল। যদিও এই কাহিনী নথিভুক্ত করা যায় না, স্তবকে এমন অনেক গুরুত্বপূর্ণ সিদ্ধান্তমূলক ইঙ্গিত রয়েছে যা একটি বিষণ্ণ হৃদয় প্রতিফলিত করে—যেমন দ্বিতীয় স্তবকে “চমকানো মশাল” এবং “ঋণপ্রাপ্ত রশ্মি”, তৃতীয় স্তবকে “বৃষ্টির মধ্য দিয়ে রংধনু সন্ধান” এবং শেষ স্তবকে “ক্রুস”।

ভাগ্যক্রমে, ড. ম্যাথিসন নিজে এই স্তবক রচনার একটি বর্ণনা দিয়েছেন:

“আমার স্তবকটি ইননেলান ম্যানসে 6 জুন, 1882-র সন্ধ্যায় রচিত। আমি তখন একা ছিলাম। সেটি আমার বোনের বিবাহের দিন ছিল, এবং বাকী পরিবার গ্লাসগোতে রাত কাটাচ্ছিল। আমার সাথে এমন একটি ঘটনা ঘটল, যা কেবল আমারই জানা ছিল, এবং যা আমাকে সবচেয়ে তীব্র মানসিক কষ্ট দিয়েছিল। এই স্তবক সেই কষ্টের ফল এবং আমার জীবনে আমি যে দ্রুত কাজ করেছি তার মধ্যে এটি ছিল সবচেয়ে দ্রুত। একটি খাঁটি অনুপ্রেরণা—আমার অনুভূতিতে এটি নিজে থেকে রচনা করার চেয়ে অন্তরের কণ্ঠের দ্বারা আমাকে অনুবাদ করে দেওয়ার মতো ছিল। আমি পুরোপুরি নিশ্চিত যে পুরো কাজটি পাঁচ মিনিটে সম্পন্ন হয়েছিল এবং একইভাবে নিশ্চিত যে আমার হাতে এতে কোনো স্পর্শ বা সংশোধন হয়নি। আমার কোনো স্বাভাবিক ছন্দের প্রতিভা নেই। আমি যা অন্যান্য সব স্তবক লিখেছি সেগুলো কারিগরি নিবন্ধ; এটি স্বর্গভূমি থেকে উদিত হওয়া দিনের অরুণোদয়ের মতো হয়ে এলো। আমি আর কখনও একই জ্বরের মতো ছন্দে লিখতে সক্ষম হইনি।”

এই স্তবক প্রথম প্রকাশিত হয় চার্চ অব স্কটল্যান্ডের মাসিক ম্যাগাজিন লাইফ অ্যান্ড ওয়ার্ক-এ, জানুয়ারি 1883-এ। সুর এক বছর পর তৎকালীন একজন বিশিষ্ট স্কটিশ অর্গানিস্ট আলবার্ট এল. পিস দ্বারা রচিত হয়েছিল; তাঁকে বিশেষভাবে ম্যাথিসনের লেখার জন্য একটি সুর রচনা করতে চাওয়া হয়েছিল।

পিস নিজের লেখায় সুর রচনার বর্ণনা এভাবে দিয়েছেন: “এটি সতর্কতার সাথে পড়ার পরে, আমি সঙ্গীতটি সরাসরি রচনা করলাম, এবং বলি যে প্রথম নোটের কালি শুকানোর আগেই আমি সুরটি শেষ করে ফেলেছিলাম।” সুরের উৎস বা নাম সেন্ট মার্গারেট সম্পর্কে নিশ্চিত কিছু জানা যায় না; এটি স্কটল্যান্ডে অত্যন্ত সম্মানিত একটি নাম, এবং নিঃসন্দেহে প্রিয় রাজকুমারী মার্গারেটের কারণে প্রাসঙ্গিক।

ম্যাথিসনের জীবনের পরবর্তী বছরগুলি—বয়স 57 থেকে 64 বছর বয়সে মৃত্যু পর্যন্ত—তিনি কিছু অতি উৎকৃষ্ট ভক্তি-লেখায় ব্যয় করেন, যার মধ্যে রয়েছে মোমেন্টস অন দ্য মাউন্ট, ভয়েস অফ দ্য স্পিরিট, এবং রেস্টস বাই দ্য রিভার। যদিও এটি বেশিরভাগ স্তবকসংগ্রহে তাঁর একমাত্র স্তবক হিসেবে পাওয়া যায়, তিনি আরও কয়েকটি সুসজ্জিত স্তবক লিখেছেন, যার মধ্যে রয়েছে “Make Me A Captive Lord” এবং “Then I Shall Be Free.”

“ও প্রেম, যা আমাকে ছেড়ে যায় না”-র চারটি মূল শব্দ হল: প্রেম, আলো, আনন্দ, এবং ক্রুস। এই শব্দগুলোকে এমন সম্পূর্ণ তৃপ্তি হিসেবে বর্ণনা করা হয়েছে যা কোনো বিশ্বাসীর জন্য যথেষ্ট, যার জীবন সম্পূর্ণরূপে ঈশ্বরের ইচ্ছায় নিবেদিত। এই চারটি অভিব্যক্তির ব্যক্তিগত তাৎপর্য আবিষ্কার করতে একজনের জীবনবাকি সময়ও লাগতে পারে।

Jehoshaphat was in trouble. He had just heard the news that a great multitude was coming to fight against him. At that moment he did what all of us naturally do when a multitude of problems come against us. He was afraid. How well I know the feeling of fear, the dread that grips my heart at times. Sometimes it’s the big things, like being misunderstood and misused, or the fear and pain of sickness, or the death of a loved one. Sometimes it’s small things, like loneliness on a Sunday afternoon. This is not comfortable, God, and I’m afraid.

Jehoshaphat laid his fear aside, set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all the land of Judah – verse 3. Even in this seemingly impossible situation of having thousands of men on their way to destroy him and his people, he fell before the Lord and acknowledged His perfect, omnipotent rule. And [he] said, O LORD God of our fathers, art not thou God in heaven? and rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen? and in thine hand is there not power and might, so that none is able to withstand thee? –verse 6.

The choice is mine. I wrestle with my own fearful thoughts, turning them over and over in my mind as if hoping to change the situation with my messy and fearful concoctions. Clinging to my fear gives me a feeling of being in control. But it is killing me from the inside out, even without the dreaded “what ifs” becoming reality. Finally, I let go and fall exhausted at my Lord’s feet, and my heart echoes the words of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah.

In humble entreaty, Jehoshaphat acknowledges their weakness and need for God’s power. O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. –verse 12.

Yes, God, I am nothing in the grand scheme of things. I have no power, not even to be the fruitful worker in Your kingdom that I always dreamed of being. I can’t fight this battle.

Jehoshaphat realized that he alone, as one man, had no strength. He called all the people of Judah together, And all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children –verse 13. They knew the strength in unity. As they stood before the Lord, waiting for Him to speak, the Spirit of the Lord came down and God gave them the words of help and hope that they were desperate for.

…Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s –verse 15. Often I try to fight my battles inside of myself rather than making myself vulnerable to others. But, as soon as I invite others into my life and into my battles, I find the strength of God through His people. When we are confused and disillusioned, we need the people of God. When we all pray together, we will get an answer to our prayer for direction.

Jehoshaphat heard the next directive from God. Tomorrow go ye down against them … Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD … fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you –verses 16-17. These words comfort my heart. Often the easiest thing to do is try to fix things, to quickly come up with a remedy of some sort to get myself out of this dilemma, to try to convince myself that everything will be okay. But God tells my heart to sit still without fear and let Him do the fighting. This takes more spiritual muscle than all the action, all the doing, and all the worrying; plus, it accomplishes a lot more.

And Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshipping the LORD –verse 18. If I obey and trust instead of worry and sit still instead of jumping into the middle of things, then I will see God do miracles. No, not always in changing my circumstances or removing all the hard things, but He does a miracle in my own soul which changes my focus and attitude. And that causes me to worship because it’s a miracle which only the all-mighty, all-powerful God can do.

Do you think any of them slept that night? They knew a fearsome army was on its way to destroy them and yet… they had heard God speak. Just perhaps there was a joyful expectation in their hearts and an eager anticipation to see how God was going to win this battle. When I learn to practice trust in the little things and the big things that pile into my life, I will soon learn to have a heart of excited expectation, because I know He is going to do something! He is going to give me a way out. Even if the worst happens, He will show my heart the way of peace and He has promised to be with me through it all. And after all, the ultimate victory is already won, so what do all these infractions really have to do with my peace and joy? Nothing.

Morning dawned; it was the day God had told them to go out against these enemies. They arose with no delay. They all knew obedience was paramount in receiving God’s blessing that day. And as they went out of the city, Jehoshaphat exhorted them. And they rose early in the morning, …and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, …Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper. And… he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army… – verses 21-20. He appointed singers to sing as they went, proclaiming to everyone and to the opposing army that they were on the Lord’s side.

I would have liked to see that huge army going out of the city, singing. They were facing a daunting task and one that would have made the strongest man tremble, but they were singing. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set… [an ambush] against the children of Ammon, [and] Moab, …which were come against Judah; and they were smitten …every one helped to destroy another –verses 22-23.

The people of Judah went to their watch tower and in amazement saw that their enemies had destroyed each other, and they saw nothing but an army of dead bodies. When a fearsome battle is set in array against me, I can still make the decision to trust and sing. Singing is a deliberate act of worship; it reminds our own souls and the souls of everyone listening that the Lord, He is God. He is the One in complete charge of my circumstances, of my tiny world, and all its problems. Suddenly the enemies are dead. The circumstances may not have changed, but the battle is finished in my soul.

The army of Judah spent the next three days gathering the riches and spoils from the dead bodies of their enemies, collecting so much that they couldn’t carry it all away with them. Astonishing! But that is how it is every time. My spirit benefits from the hard things that I endure successfully. Each victory allows me to collect ‘spoils’ which will profit me for the rest of my life. My heart is full of blessing, of being cared for, and being carried by a Heavenly Father. The “armies of Moab and Ammon” have brought blessing instead of ruin.

They came again to their homes in Jerusalem with singing, and harps, and trumpets, overloaded with all their spoil. The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of the land when they heard how God had fought this huge battle, then Jehoshaphat’s realm was quiet. Peace reigned.

The peace of knowing that all I really need is God and His working in my life is the ultimate peace. This broken world can bring all manner of pain, sickness, and disappointments, but God brings rest to the heart that was once so full of tumult and fear. There is rest ‘round about’ and all the ‘kingdoms of the land’ will be amazed and curious at the strength that is within us, because it is the strength that no one can match—the strength of our amazing God.

Jehoshafat was in die moeilikheid. Hy het so pas die nuus gehoor dat ’n geweldige menigte op pad is om teen hom te veg. Op daardie oomblik het hy gedoen wat ons almal natuurlik doen wanneer ’n menigte probleme teen ons opkom. Hy was angstig. Hoe goed ken ek die gevoel van vrees, die benoudheid wat soms my hart gryp. Soms is dit die groot dinge, soos verkeerd verstaan en misbruik word, of die vrees en pyn van siekte, of die dood van ’n geliefde. Soms is dit klein dinge, soos eensaamheid op ’n Sondagmiddag. Dit is nie gerieflik nie, God, en ek is bang.

Jehoshafat het sy vrees ter syde gesit, homself toegelê om die Here te soek, en het ’n vas afgekondig deur die hele land van Juda – verse 3. Selfs in hierdie skynbaar onmoontlike situasie waar duisende mans op pad was om hom en sy volk te vernietig, het hy voor die Here neergeval en Sy volmaakte, almagtige heerskappy erken. En hy het gesê: HERE, God van ons vaders, is U nie God in die hemel nie? Heers U nie oor al die koninkryke van die heidene nie? Is daar nie krag en sterkte in U hand nie, sodat niemand U kan ondermyn nie? –verse 6.

Die keuse is myne. Ek worstel met my eie vrese gedagtes, keer dit oor en oor in my gedagtes asof ek hoop om die situasie met my gemors en bangsiende mengsels te verander. Vasklou aan my vrees gee vir my ’n gevoel van beheer. Maar dit maak my van binne uit dood, selfs al word die gevreesde “wat as”-scenario’s nie werklik nie. Uiteindelik los ek dit en val uitgeput by my Here se voete, en my hart eggo die woorde van Jehoshafat, die koning van Juda.

In nederige smeekgebed erken Jehoshafat hulle swakheid en behoefte aan God se krag. O ons God, sal U hulle nie oordeel nie? Want ons het geen krag teen hierdie geweldige menigte wat teen ons kom nie; en ons weet nie wat om te doen nie; maar ons oë is op U gerig. –verse 12.

Ja, God, ek is niks in die groot prentjie van dinge nie. Ek het geen krag nie, nie eers om die vrugbare werker in U koninkryk te wees waarvan ek altyd gedroom het nie. Ek kan nie hierdie stryd voer nie.

Jehoshafat het besef dat hy alleen, as een man, geen krag gehad het nie. Hy het al die mense van Juda bymekaar geroep, En heel Juda het voor die HERE aangestaan, met hulle klein kinders, hulle vroue en hulle kinders –verse 13. Hulle het die krag van eenheid geken. Terwyl hulle voor die Here gestaan en gewag het dat Hy sou spreek, het die Gees van die Here neergedaal en God het vir hulle die woorde van hulp en hoop gegee waarna hulle so wanhopig was.

…Moet nie vrees of bevrees wees weens hierdie geweldige menigte nie; want die stryd is nie julle s’n nie, maar God s’n –verse 15. Dikwels probeer ek my gevegte binne myself voer in plaas daarvan om myself bloot te maak aan ander. Maar sodra ek ander in my lewe en in my stryd nooi, vind ek God se krag deur Sy mense. Wanneer ons verward en ontgoocheld is, het ons die mense van God nodig. Wanneer ons almal saam bid, sal ons ’n antwoord op ons gebed vir leiding ontvang.

Jehoshafat het die volgende opdrag van God gehoor. Môre, gaan julle teen hulle af … Julle sal nie nodig hê om in hierdie stryd te veg nie: stel julle neer, staan stil, en sien die heil van die HERE … vrees nie en wees nie ontsteld nie; môre gaan uit teen hulle: want die HERE sal by julle wees –verses 16-17. Hierdie woorde vertroos my hart. Dikwels is die maklikste ding om te doen om dinge reg te stel, vinnig ’n oplossing te vind om myself uit hierdie benoudheid te kry, om myself te probeer oortuig dat alles goed sal wees. Maar God sê vir my hart om stil te sit sonder vrees en Hom die geveg te laat voer. Dit verg meer geestelike spierkrag as al die aksie, al die doen en al die bekommernis; en tog bereik dit soveel meer.

En Jehoshafat het sy kop gebuig en sy gesig tot die grond neergeslaan: en al Juda en die inwoners van Jerusalem het voor die HERE geval en hom aanbid –verse 18. As ek gehoorsaam is en vertrou in plaas van bekommer en stil sit in plaas van om in die middel van dinge te spring, sal ek sien dat God wonders doen. Nee, nie altyd om my omstandighede te verander of al die moeilike dinge weg te neem nie, maar Hy doen ’n wonder in my eie siel wat my fokus en houding verander. En dit laat my aanbid, want dit is ’n wonder wat net die almagtige, al-kragtige God kan doen.

Dink jy hulle het daardie nag slaap gekry? Hulle het geweet ’n vreesaanjaende leër was op pad om hulle te vernietig en tog… hulle het God hoor spreek. Miskien was daar ’n blye verwagting in hulle harte en ’n gretige spanning om te sien hoe God hierdie stryd sou wen. Wanneer ek leer om vertroue te beoefen in die klein dinge en die groot dinge wat in my lewe opstapel, sal ek gou leer om ’n hart van opgewonde verwagting te hê, omdat ek weet Hy gaan iets doen! Hy gaan vir my ’n uitweg gee. Selfs as die ergste gebeur, sal Hy my hart die weg van vrede wys en Hy het belowe om deur alles by my te wees. En ná alles is die uiteindelike oorwinning reeds behaal, so wat het al hierdie oortredings regtig met my vrede en vreugde te doen? Niks.

Die oggend het aangebreek; dit was die dag wat God vir hulle gesê het om uit te gaan teen hierdie vyande. Hulle het sonder uitstel opgestaan. Hulle het almal geweet dat gehoorsaamheid van die hoogste belang was om daardie dag God se seën te ontvang. En toe hulle uit die stad uitgaan, het Jehoshafat hulle aangespoor. En hulle het vroeg in die oggend opgestaan, …en toe hulle gegaan het, het Jehoshafat gestaan en gesê, …Glo in die HERE julle God, en julle sal gevestig wees; glo sy profete, en julle sal voorspoedig wees. En… hy het sangers aangestel vir die HERE, wat die skoonheid van heiligheid moes loof, terwyl hulle voor die leër uit optrek… –verse 21-20. Hy het sangers aangestel om te sing terwyl hulle gegaan het, en aan almal en aan die vyandige leër te verklaar dat hulle aan die Here se kant was.

Ek sou graag die groot leër uit die stad sien uitgaan, singende. Hulle het ’n afskrikwekkende taak voorgehad wat die sterkste man sou doen bewerig, maar hulle het gesing. En toe hulle begin sing en lof loof, het die HERE ’n [oorval] gestel teen die kinders van Ammon en Moab … wat teen Juda gekom het; en hulle is geslaan …en elkeen het gehelp om die ander te vernietig –verses 22-23.

Die mense van Juda het na hulle wagtorings gegaan en met verstomming gesien dat hul vyande mekaar vernietig het, en hulle het niks anders gesien nie as ’n leër dooie liggame. Wanneer ’n vreesaanjaende stryd teen my opgerig word, kan ek steeds die besluit neem om te vertrou en te sing. Sing is ’n doelbewuste daad van aanbidding; dit herinner ons eie siel en die siele van almal wat luister dat die Here, Hy is God. Hy is Die Een wat totaal beheer het oor my omstandighede, my klein wêreld en al sy probleme. Skielik is die vyande dood. Die omstandighede mag nie verander het nie, maar die stryd is klaar in my siel.

Die leër van Juda het die volgende drie dae spandeer om die rykdomme en buit van die dooie liggame van hul vyande in te samel, so veel dat hulle dit nie alles kon wegdra nie. Verstommend! Maar dit is hoe dit elke keer gaan. My gees baat by die moeilike dinge wat ek suksesvol deurstaan. Elke oorwinning stel my in staat om ‘buit’ in te samel wat my die res van my lewe sal bevoordeel. My hart is vol seën, vol sorg en gedra word deur ’n Hemelse Vader. Die “legers van Moab en Ammon” het seën gebring in plaas van verwoesting.

Hulle het weer huistoe gekom in Jerusalem, singende, met harpe en trompette, oorlaai met al hulle buit. Die vrees van God het op al die koninkryke van die land geval toe hulle gehoor het hoe God hierdie groot stryd gevoer het; toe het Jehoshafat se gebied stil geraak. Vrede het gehersk.

Die vrede om te weet dat alles wat ek regtig nodig het God is en Sy werking in my lewe is die uiteindelike vrede. Hierdie gebroke wêreld kan allerhande pyn, siekte en teleurstellings bring, maar God bring rus aan die hart wat eens so vol gewoel en vrees was. Daar is rus rondom, en al die “koninkryke van die land” sal verbaas en nuuskierig wees oor die krag wat in ons is, want dit is die krag wat niemand kan ewears nie—die krag van ons wonderlike God.

This hymn is generally thought to be one of the most loved hymns written during the latter part of the 19th century. The writing of this thoughtful and beautifully constructed text is even more amazing when we consider that its author was one who was almost completely blind and who describes the writing of this hymn as the “fruit of much mental suffering,” and “the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life.”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, March 27, 1842, George Matheson had only partial vision as a boy, and, after entering Glasgow University, his eyesight continued to fail rapidly. Except for “moments of shadowy eyesight”, he was totally blind by the age of 18. This affliction of blindness seemed to be a tragedy since he was an eager and avid scholar, yet it caused him to trust in the Lord, and it strengthened his walk with God.

He entered the university at the early age of 15 and graduated with high honors in 1861 at the age of 19. He was a brilliant scholar, even spending four more years after graduation in more theological studies, all the while remaining single. After his graduation he became entirely dependent on others, relying much upon his two sisters, who were so dedicated that they learned Latin, Greek, and Hebrew since they thought it might aid him in his theological studies. One of them continued to be his faithful co-worker and helper throughout his life, assisting in his calling of being a pastor and other ministerial duties.

After completing his theological course, he became assistant pastor to the renowned Dr. Macduff, in whose church of thousands of members he had been brought up. Soon, however, he was chosen minister of the Church of Scotland in the seaport summer resort of Innellan. Here he stayed for eighteen years. Many families came to spend the summer there chiefly to be inspired by his preaching ministry.

Whenever he preached, the open Bible was before him as he stood in the pulpit, and to the congregation, he seemed to be reading from it. During the messages, his eyes looked straight at the congregation, and many went away with no clue that they just listened to a blind preacher. It was during this time that he made a practice of memorizing his sermons, as well as the passages of Scripture he used in his messages. His memory was so sharp that if someone read one of his prepared sermons to him twice, or whatever else he wanted to memorize, he could from then on repeat it perfectly. One Sunday, however, after doing this for 12 years, when in the middle of a powerful sermon his memory completely collapsed, and the topic on which he was preaching vanished from his mind. He sat down and commenced to request a psalm to be sung, and, after the song, with perfect calmness told the audience what had happened. With this done, he stood to his feet, gave out a new text, and preached an impromptu sermon of great power. After that experience George wrote little of his sermons, and finally prepared only an outline from which to preach.

Dr. Matheson’s final pastorate was taken up in 1886 at the age of 44 where he became pastor of the large St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, where his eloquent preaching consistently attracted large throngs of people to the services. Here he remained for 13 years, his church growing from 1,494 members to 1,703 in the first 5 years. He continued faithfully preaching the gospel and became well known as one of Scotland’s outstanding preachers and pastors and was greatly esteemed in Edinburgh where he resided.

Many speculations have been made regarding the cause of the mental distress which prompted the author to write this text. A very popular account, although never verified, is that this text was a result of the severe trial Matheson faced after his soon-to-be bride left him just before their marriage when she learned of his impending total blindness. Although this story cannot be documented, there are many significant hints in this hymn reflecting a saddened heart, such as the “flickering torch” and the “borrowed ray” in the second verse, the tracing of the “rainbow through the rain” in the third stanza, as well as the “cross” in the last verse.

Fortunately, Dr. Matheson did relate an account of his writing of this hymn:

“My hymn was composed in the manse of Innellan on the evening of June 6, 1882. I was at that time alone. It was the day of my sister’s wedding, and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow. Something happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering and was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. A genuine inspiration, I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes and equally sure it never received at my hands any retouching or correction. I have no natural gift of rhythm. All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

Este himno suele considerarse uno de los más queridos compuestos durante la segunda mitad del siglo 19º. La redacción de este texto reflexivo y bellamente construido resulta aún más asombrosa si consideramos que su autor era casi completamente ciego y que describió la escritura de este himno como el “fruto de mucho sufrimiento mental” y “el trabajo más rápido que he hecho en mi vida”.

Nacido en Glasgow, Escocia, el 27 de marzo de 1842, George Matheson tenía visión parcial de niño y, después de ingresar en la Universidad de Glasgow, su vista siguió fallando rápidamente. Excepto por “momentos de vista sombría”, quedó totalmente ciego a los 18 años. Esta aflicción de ceguera pareció una tragedia ya que era un estudioso entusiasta y ávido, pero le llevó a confiar en el Señor y fortaleció su caminar con Dios.

Ingresó en la universidad a la temprana edad de 15 años y se graduó con altas calificaciones en 1861, a los 19 años. Fue un brillante erudito, incluso pasando cuatro años más después de la graduación en estudios teológicos, todo el tiempo permaneciendo soltero. Tras su graduación se volvió totalmente dependiente de otros, confiando mucho en sus dos hermanas, que estaban tan dedicadas que aprendieron latín, griego y hebreo porque pensaban que podrían ayudarle en sus estudios teológicos. Una de ellas continuó siendo su fiel colaboradora y ayudante a lo largo de su vida, auxiliándole en su ministerio pastoral y otras labores ministeriales.

Tras completar su curso teológico, se convirtió en pastor asistente del renombrado Dr. Macduff, en cuya iglesia de miles de miembros se había criado. Pronto, sin embargo, fue elegido ministro de la Iglesia de Escocia en la estación veraniega portuaria de Innellan. Allí permaneció dieciocho años. Muchas familias venían a pasar el verano allí principalmente para inspirarse con su ministerio de predicación.

Siempre que predicaba, la Biblia abierta estaba delante de él mientras se levantaba en el púlpito, y para la congregación parecía estar leyéndola. Durante los mensajes, sus ojos miraban directamente a la congregación, y muchos se marchaban sin sospechar que acababan de escuchar a un predicador ciego. Fue durante este tiempo que tomó la costumbre de memorizar sus sermones, así como los pasajes de las Escrituras que usaba en sus mensajes. Su memoria era tan aguda que si alguien le leía uno de sus sermones preparados dos veces, o cualquier otra cosa que quisiera memorizar, desde entonces podía repetirlo perfectamente. Un domingo, sin embargo, después de hacer esto durante 12 años, en medio de un poderoso sermón su memoria se vino completamente abajo y el tema sobre el que predicaba desapareció de su mente. Se sentó y comenzó a pedir que se cantara un salmo y, después del canto, con perfecta calma contó a la audiencia lo que había ocurrido. Con esto hecho, se puso de pie, dio un nuevo texto y predicó un sermón improvisado de gran poder. Después de esa experiencia George escribió poco de sus sermones y finalmente sólo preparaba un bosquejo del cual predicar.

El pastorado final del Dr. Matheson comenzó en 1886, a los 44 años, cuando se hizo pastor de la gran iglesia parroquial de St. Bernard’s en Edimburgo, donde su elocuente predicación atraía constantemente a grandes multitudes a los servicios. Allí permaneció durante 13 años, creciendo su iglesia de 1.494 miembros a 1.703 en los primeros 5 años. Continuó predicando fielmente el evangelio y llegó a ser conocido como uno de los predicadores y pastores más destacados de Escocia, y fue muy estimado en Edimburgo, donde residía.

Se han hecho muchas especulaciones sobre la causa de la angustia mental que motivó al autor a escribir este texto. Un relato muy popular, aunque nunca verificado, afirma que este texto fue resultado de la dura prueba que enfrentó Matheson después de que su prometida lo dejara poco antes del matrimonio al enterarse de su inminente ceguera total. Aunque esta historia no puede documentarse, hay muchos indicios significativos en este himno que reflejan un corazón entristecido, como la “antorcha parpadeante” y el “rayo prestado” en la segunda estrofa, el trazar el “arco iris a través de la lluvia” en la tercera estrofa, así como la “cruz” en la última estrofa.

Por fortuna, el Dr. Matheson relató un relato sobre la composición de este himno:

“Mi himno fue compuesto en la casa parroquial de Innellan en la noche del 6 de junio de 1882. En aquel momento estaba solo. Era el día de la boda de mi hermana y el resto de la familia se quedó esa noche en Glasgow. Me sucedió algo que sólo yo conocía y que me causó el más severo sufrimiento mental. El himno fue el fruto de ese sufrimiento y fue el trabajo más rápido que he hecho en mi vida. Una inspiración genuina; tuve más bien la impresión de que me fue dictado por alguna voz interior que de que yo lo hubiese elaborado. Estoy bastante seguro de que toda la obra se completó en cinco minutos y con la misma seguridad de que nunca recibió de mi mano retoque ni corrección. No tengo don natural para el ritmo. Todas las demás estrofas que he escrito son artículos manufacturados; esta vino como un amanecer desde lo alto. Nunca he podido recuperar esa misma fervor en verso.”

El himno apareció por primera vez en la revista mensual de la Iglesia de Escocia, Life and Work, en enero de 1883. La melodía fue compuesta un año después por un prominente organista escocés de su tiempo, Albert L. Peace, a quien se le pidió que escribiera una melodía especialmente para el texto de Matheson.

El propio relato de Peace sobre la composición de esta fina melodía es el siguiente: “Después de leerlo detenidamente, escribí la música de un tirón, y puedo decir que la tinta de la primera nota apenas estaba seca cuando terminé la melodía.” El origen del nombre de la melodía, St. Margaret, se desconoce, salvo que es un nombre muy venerado en Escocia, y ciertamente por la querida reina Margaret de Escocia.

Los últimos años de la vida de Matheson, desde los 57 hasta su muerte a los 64, los dedicó a escribir algunos de los más finos escritos devocionales en lengua inglesa, entre ellos Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit y Rests by the River. Aunque éste es su único himno que se encuentra en la mayoría de los himnarios, sí escribió algunos otros himnos notables, entre ellos “Make Me A Captive Lord” y “Then I Shall Be Free”.

Las cuatro palabras clave de “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” son: amor, luz, gozo y cruz. Estas palabras han sido descritas como la satisfacción completa para cualquier creyente cuya vida esté totalmente rendida a la voluntad de Dios. Podría llevar el resto de la vida descubrir por completo el significado personal de estas cuatro expresiones.

Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect. For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. …it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe –1 Corinthians –1:17-21.

The modern Christian world has duly accepted many of the lowly vehicles that God used to usher in the Kingdom. The virgin birth, the rough-hewn manger, and the swaddling clothes have become sovereign monuments that we could scarcely do without. Even the rude donkey is appreciated on Good Friday and the old, rugged cross has become a spiritual emblem nominally displayed on neck chains and ornate pulpit carvings. While man remains infatuated with the traditional symbols of the gospel, there remains an absurd avenue of God’s choosing that is becoming increasingly despised.

For centuries, the Gospel was heralded by foolish and unlearned men (according to their elite and intellectual counterparts). The biblical truth spoken in simplicity was sufficient of itself for God’s Holy Spirit to use to convert the sinner. While there is no lack for preaching in these days, it appears that much of it is of a different sort than the original form that Christ exemplified. If anyone was capable of articulating a flourish of orations in an accurate philosophical language it would have been the Apostle Paul. Yet, he refused to preach the gospel in this manner, …lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect –1 Corinthians 1:17. He preached carefully, lest the success should be ascribed to the force of art, and not of truth itself.

Paul had been ingrained in Jewish learning at the feet of Gamaliel and was affluent in understanding both Hebrew and Greek, but in preaching the cross of Christ, he laid his learning aside. He spoke the words of the Gospel in a language void of human power lest the honor belonging to Christ be eclipsed by his own personal power. For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible –2 Corinthians 10:10. It is here where the modern church has spurned the meager vehicles chosen by Christ and the Apostles while diverting to a route more acceptable to in our day. Modern day efficiency demands a more direct route to the end, and if the Bible doesn’t forbid it, we feel that it is our prerogative to employ it.

While evangelical films, music concerts, and a host of other questionable venues of ministry could be mentioned, I wish to speak primarily to the modern invitation system known as the “altar call”. While it is commonly associated with the “old fashioned meetings” of the past two centuries, it is indeed modern due to the fact that for nearly nineteen centuries no one had ever heard of the practice. Evangelists such as George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards, and even John Wesley had never heard of such a custom. Even Charles Spurgeon (heralded as the “Prince of Preachers”) strongly criticized it and refused to adopt it.*

Thus, we observe, the practice was not born in the apostolic church. It is not found in the ministry of Jesus, His apostles, or even the church of the post-apostolic period. We do see Jesus and the apostles inviting men and women to come to Christ and to be saved, but never by means of this particular method. So why has this practice become such an essential tool in most evangelical and in many Anabaptist churches today? The answer—pragmatic results. Immediately following the sermon, the congregation will sing a hymn during which the preacher calls men and women to walk to the front of the auditorium (to the “altar”) to make a public decision for Christ. Salvation is offered to all who will but come to the front and receive it. Those who come often receive the personal attention of a counselor to pray with them and lead them through confession.

This practice was designed to encourage decisions and obtain results. So, it did. And with slight variations the new method spread with increasing popularity through Charles Finney, and later, Dwight L. Moody, and finally, into virtually all of nineteenth and twentieth century evangelicalism. Peter Cartwright, Sam Jones, R. A. Torrey, Billy Sunday, Bob Jones, Gipsy Smith, John R. Rice, Billy Graham, and George Brunk all employed the method with impressive success. Thus, the invitation system became the accepted normal practice and those who question it are often deemed spiritually eccentric.

Why should we take issue with the practice if the scripture doesn’t forbid it? The answer lies in the question of the propriety of the invitation system. Let us first note that the Scriptures abound with invitations to salvation. Such offers as, Come unto me, …and I will give you rest –Matthew 11:28, and, …If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink –John 7:37, are marvelous offers of life to those who will trust Christ. The apostles also did not hesitate to show forth Christ as Savior to all who would listen to their message.

They preached indiscriminately, Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out… –Acts 3:19, and …we pray you in Christ›s stead, be ye reconciled to God –2 Corinthians 5:20. And they testified …to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ –Acts 20:21. With all this, every Christian should not only agree but also rejoice.

Finally, …compel them to come in, that my house may be filled –Luke 14:23, is another Bible verse which could be used to lend support to the altar call method. Still, this says nothing to bolster the correctness of the altar call. As we examine the practice at its roots, we cannot help but observe a few deficiencies:

…Extra-Biblical

This is no reflection upon the multitudes who have found salvation at such an event. The angels in heaven rejoice at the repentance of every sinner no matter how he arrives there. We simply wish to hold forth the simplicity of the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. The altar call is used as a specific addition to the sermon to bring to fruition what the foolishness of preaching itself could not do.

The altar call gained popularity in the 1830’s with the preaching of Charles G. Finney who wrote, “A revival is not a miracle, or dependent on a miracle, in any sense. It is a purely philosophical result of the right use of the constituted means.” ** We cannot accuse all who practice the altar call of believing this, but it is rather revealing that the preacher who brought it to popularity seemed to liken it more to a mathematical equation than to divine involvement.

When the truth falls on the soil of a good and honest heart, the seed veritably takes root and produces fruit. This seed of truth needs no artificial dress. It shines out with the greatest majesty in its own light and prevails in the world by its divine authority. It is a demonstration of the Spirit, without need of human invention or intervention. The plain preaching of a crucified Christ is more powerful than all the oratory, philosophical, and heart gripping modes of the world.

…Emotional Thrust

The altar call requires a seeker to leave his seat and walk to the forefront for pardon. These invitations are often preceded by fearfully moving accounts, sad stories, or testimonies that stir the emotions to fear, guilt, or regret. Flanked by a soft hymn sung by the congregation, the emotions are ripe to move forward. Those who choose to repent from their seat without responding are often esteemed as “missing an opportunity”.

And these are they likewise which are sown on stony ground; who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness; And have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word’s sake, immediately they are offended –Mark 4:16-17. We refuse to deduce that all who were converted under this type of ministry are stony ground hearers. Yet, the vast majority of those who receive it in such a charged emotional environment will often have a less than sincere conversion.

I once had an exuberant client in my shop who informed me that their church had sponsored a national evangelical ministry to preach at the public high school. “There were over 400 decisions for Christ!” While we all wish to rejoice with the angels, one cannot but question how many of them were still in church a year later. While the lack of true commitment may not fall upon the use of the altar call alone, we may be sure that the seed so quick to spring up will surely manifest itself at the moorings of an emotional invitation. Those that have no root would be better off never having responded prematurely.

Conversions wrought through emotional channels are often questionable and transient. Holy Spirit promptings do not need human strength, wisdom, or efforts to convey them forth. Revival methods such as shouting, overt weeping, emotion eliciting music, and the telling of sentimental stories is the man-made art of preaching. It is also found in many other public venues that are designed to elicit a specific predetermined response from the hearer. Each of these dimensions is quite natural to human behavior and, at times, there may be a fine line between what is acceptable and unacceptable in preaching. Great care should be taken that we do not create an emotional climax and eclipse the message in an inordinate manner lest the power be of men and not of Christ.

…Encroachment to Parental and Local Church Authority

Children are often a target at such a time. They may feel guilty for some childish misdeed, but a fiery message followed by emotional pleading can be very unsettling. These are times when a parent should speak to the heart of their child and connect in a spiritual way. Instead, often the child is moved to the front and given a church counselor for them to pour out their confession.

I know a woman whose father was an itinerant evangelical preacher. She claims that she responded “hundreds of times” to the altar call. A casual and honest appraisal would reveal that while the altar call may bring commencement to many sincere conversions, it also avails itself equally to a host of premature decisions and pressure-driven commitments. This often leaves many unstable souls wallowing in spiritual instability and struggling with a lack of assurance of salvation for years to come.

For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel. Wherefore I beseech you, be ye followers of me –1 Corinthians 4:15-16. God has ordained fathers and mothers to bring birth to their children, both physical and spiritual.

Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ –1 Corinthians 11:1. The skilled itinerant evangelist has no intention of begetting spiritual children and making followers of himself. This he leaves to others, for he has found his gift in compelling people to make decisions.

And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you; And to esteem them very highly in love for their work’s sake… –1 Thessalonians 5:13. But there is to be a God-given loyalty to those spiritual fathers who labor over us and bring us to birth beyond the many instructors upon life’s pathway. The contemporary emergence of thousands of “hit and run” ministries should cause us concern.

While public confession of sin is obviously an important doctrine of Christ to accompany salvation, these confessions belong in the hands of the spiritual authorities who can discern the situation and help further the soul through tomorrow’s temptations. When those who know the convert are personally engaged, a more thorough and honest examination can be employed to bring about a sincere conversion. This will lay the groundwork for the deep digging required to lay the foundation upon the Rock and establish the soul, both in the home and in the church.

…Engineered Faith

When people are continually subject to revival scenes, there is often an unspoken expectation that the meetings are the place to do business with God. This has a tendency to confuse “saving faith” with a “saving act”. The emphasis on “coming forward to receive Christ” confuses the meaning of faith. Christ is the strong consolation, to whom we … have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast… –Hebrews 6:18-19.(emphasis mine)

The invitation of Christ to …Come unto me… Matthew 11:28, should never be confused with “coming to the altar” (walking to the front). The foolishness of preaching is the invitation, and “Christ” is the destination. The power of the oration shall not lie in the dynamics of the preacher but within the truth of the message. We become like paper figures, having no power at all in ourselves. All power must come from above; all methods used must also come from above. –Watchman Nee ***

The wind bloweth where it listeth… John 3:8, likewise the Holy Spirit, and the preacher must be content with that. I trust that many who give altar calls have the best of intentions and do not wish to circumvent the Spirit. But most works accomplished in the apex of emotion have a strong inclination to be fallacious. So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God –Romans 10:17.

Endnotes:

* “Charles Spurgeon, well known for his evangelistic abilities, firmly refused to adopt the practice of altar calls and he severely criticized it. He viewed the altar call as a method to force decisions as results, but he recognized its potential abuse and dangers.” Altar Calls – Bill Brenner

‘I should like to go into the enquiry-room.’ I dare say you would, but we are not willing to pander to popular superstition. We fear that in those rooms men are warmed into a fictitious confidence. Very few of the supposed converts of enquiry-rooms turn out well. Go to your God at once, even where you now are. Cast yourself on Christ, at once, ere you stir an inch!’ - Pleading and Encouragement – Charles Haddon Spurgeon – Aug 17, 1841

** What A Revival Of Religion Is – Charles Grandison Finney – The Belknap Press Of Harvard University A “Revival of Religion” presupposes a declension. Almost all the religion in the world has been produced by revivals. God has found it necessary to take advantage of the excitability there is in mankind, to produce powerful excitements among them, before he can lead them to obey. Men are so sluggish, there are so many things to lead their minds off from religion, and to oppose the influence of the gospel that it is necessary to raise an excitement among them, till the tide rises so high as to sweep away the opposing obstacles. They must be so excited that they will break over these counteracting influences, before they will obey God.

*** Spirit Force vs. Psychic Force – Watchman Nee
