Lunchtime was over and it was that delightful hour of the day when mom said it was time for a break. Since Ellie was ten, she wasn’t required to take a daily nap anymore, so she set about trying to decide just how she would spend this free time. She loved being outdoors, so the sunny skies and fresh air of this particularly lovely summer day fairly pulled her outside.

“I know!” she thought to herself. “This would be a perfect time to try some whittling with that knife Paul gave me.”

She had spent a week with her aunt and uncle who lived several counties over from hers and while there, her cousin Paul had given her a knife that he had made. It had a short, round handle and he had inserted a small piece of steel into one end. He then honed the blade to a nice sharp edge. He could carve the funniest little faces on small blocks of wood and Ellie was always eager to see what he would create next. She tried to copy him, but it didn’t seem as if she would be turning out anything very exciting any time soon. Still, it was fun to try, so she got the knife from her drawer in her bedroom and headed outside.

The large maple tree in front of their old stone farmhouse beckoned to her. Its low hanging branches seemed like the perfect place to perch and try out that knife again. Ellie selected a few large twigs and then hoisted herself up into the cool shade of the tree. Once situated, she began cutting and picking away at her pieces of wood. She still couldn’t make eyes and a nose appear, but she had fun carving notches and shaving off small pieces of bark. It was a relaxing thing with which to be occupied while enjoying the quietness of the afternoon. She was so glad this tree was in their yard, and she was so glad that Paul had given her that whittling knife.

After a time, the branch Ellie was sitting on began to feel rough and hard, and the twigs she was whittling had nearly disappeared. “I should go see what the boys are doing,” she thought. She shifted to the lowest branch and sat poised, ready to jump down like she always did to get out of the tree.

She paused, looking at the knife in her hand. “Never jump down from anywhere while holding a knife in your hand!” her mother’s voice rang in her memory. “It is a very dangerous thing to do. You could get cut very badly.” Ellie sat thinking about that for a little.

“Yes, I know that’s probably true,” she told herself. “But I think if I am very careful, I could jump down and it will be fine,” she reasoned.

She firmly grasped the knife in her right hand, then quickly jumped the distance to the ground. Just as she landed, her ankle turned and gave way under her. She fell awkwardly onto her left leg. And, oh no! That little knife had plunged into her left wrist as she was trying to keep her balance. She quickly pulled it out and watched, with her heart beating rapidly, as the blood welled up, dark and warm. It was a small cut, only about one quarter of an inch long, but it had gone in rather deeply.

What should she do now? Yes, there was no doubt about it, her mom had been right after all! In her heart, she knew the right thing to do would be to go directly to her mother and tell her what she had done. But she felt guilty and ashamed. She had known better than to jump down with that knife, yet she had gone ahead and done it anyway. Guiltily, she quickly pressed her thumb on top of the wound and slipped into the house. The bleeding soon stopped, and after finding a little bandage and placing it on her cut, she quietly put her knife away and found a book to read. She never told her mom what she had done until many years later when she was a grown woman.

Today, as she looks at that scar, which is still visible from 40 years ago, she wonders why God had protected her. She had been a foolish little girl to not go immediately to her mother and confess what she had done. She could have gotten a severe infection from getting cut with a dirty, slightly rusty knife. Even though she acted foolishly, she is grateful that God protected her, but she still wishes she had confessed her disobedience to her mother.

It is never wise to hide anything from your parents. They need to know those wrong things you do, no matter how embarrassed or ashamed you might feel. Parents need to know all the things that happen to their children It is God’s design for fathers and mothers to be there for their children, to help you when you get hurt, and to guide and teach you as you learn how to be good, obedient children. God’s way is always the best.

Lunchtyd was verby en dit was daardie genotvolle uur van die dag toe ma gesê het dit is tyd vir ’n rus. Omdat Ellie tien was, moes sy nie meer daagliks ’n middagslapie hou nie, so sy het besin oor hoe sy hierdie vrye tyd sou deurbring. Sy het daarvan gehou om buite te wees, en die sonnige hemel en vars lug van hierdie besonder mooi somersdag het haar haastig buite toe getrek.

“Ek weet!” het sy by haarself gedink. “Dit sal ’n perfekte tyd wees om bietjie te kerf met daardie mes wat Paul my gegee het.”

Sy het ’n week by haar tannie en oom gebly wat ’n paar dorpe verder van hulle af gewoon het, en terwyl sy daar was, het haar neef Paul vir haar ’n mes gegee wat hy gemaak het. Dit het ’n kort, ronde handvatsel gehad en hy het ’n klein stuk staal in een kant ingesit. Hy het toe die lem tot ’n mooi skerp rand geslyp. Hy kon die snaakste gesiggie op klein houtblokkies kerf en Ellie was altyd gretig om te sien wat hy volgende sou maak. Sy het probeer om hom na te doen, maar dit het nie gelyk of sy binnekort iets besonders op die been sou bring nie. Tog was dit lekker om te probeer, so sy het die mes uit haar kasie in haar slaapkamer gehaal en na buite gegaan.

Die groot esdoringboom voor hulle ou kliphuisie het na haar gelok. Sy laag hangende takke het gelyk na die perfekte plek om te gaan sit en weer daardie mes uit te toets. Ellie het ’n paar groot takkies uitgekies en haarself dan in die koel skadu van die boom opgehef. Sodra sy gesetel was, het sy begin sny en wegkrap aan haar stukke hout. Sy kon steeds nie oë en ’n neus laat voorkom nie, maar sy het pret gehad toe sy kerfbane gemaak en klein stukkies bas afgeskuur het. Dit was ’n ontspanne ding om mee besig te wees terwyl sy die stilte van die middag geniet het. Sy was so bly hierdie boom was in hulle tuin, en sy was so bly Paul het vir haar daardie kerfmes gegee.

Na ’n rukkie het die tak waarop Ellie gesit het, hard en growwe begin voel, en die takkies wat sy gekerf het, was amper weg. “Ek moet gaan sien wat die seuns doen,” het sy gedink. Sy het na die laagste tak geskuif en gesit, gereed om af te spring soos sy gewoonlik doen om uit die boom te kom.

Sy het stilgehou en na die mes in haar hand gekyk. “Moet nooit van waar ook al af spring terwyl jy ’n mes in jou hand hou nie!” het haar ma se stem in haar geheue geklink. “Dis ’n baie gevaarlike ding om te doen. Jy kan baie sleg gesny raak.” Ellie het ’n rukkie daaroor gedink.

“Ja, ek weet dit is waarskynlik waar,” het sy vir haarself gesê. “Maar ek dink as ek baie versigtig is, kan ek afspring en dit sal in orde wees,” het sy beredeneer.

Sy het die mes stewig in haar regterhand vasgegryp en toe vinnig die afstand na die grond afgespring. Net toe sy land, het haar enkel omgedraai en verkrummel. Sy het ongemaklik op haar linkerbeen geval. En, o nee! Daardie klein mes het in haar linkerpols ingedring terwyl sy probeer om haar balans te behou. Sy het dit vinnig uitgetrek en met ’n vinnig kloppende hart dopgehou hoe die bloed opwel, donker en warm. Dit was ’n klein sny, net ongeveer ’n kwart duim lank, maar dit het redelik diep ingegaan.

Wat moes sy nou doen? Ja, daar was geen twyfel nie, haar ma was tog reg! In haar hart het sy geweet die regte ding sou wees om reguit na haar ma toe te gaan en te vertel wat sy gedoen het. Maar sy het skuldig en geskaam gevoel. Sy het geweet sy moes nie met daardie mes afspring nie, tog het sy dit tog gedoen. Skuldig het sy vinnig haar duim op die wond gedruk en die huis ingesluip. Die bloeding het gou opgehou, en nadat sy ’n klein pleister gevind en op haar sny geplak het, het sy stilweg haar mes weggesteek en ’n boek gaan lees. Sy het haar ma eers baie jare later vertel wat sy gedoen het, toe sy ’n volwasse vrou was.

Vandag, wanneer sy na daardie litteken kyk, wat nog steeds sigbaar is van 40 jaar gelede, wonder sy waarom God haar beskerm het. Sy was ’n dwase klein meisie om nie dadelik na haar ma te gaan en te bely wat sy gedoen het nie. Sy kon ’n ernstige infeksie gekry het van ’n vuil, effens roesige mes. Al het sy dwaas opgetree, is sy dankbaar dat God haar beskerm het, maar sy wens steeds dat sy haar ongehoorsaamheid aan haar ma bely het.

Dit is nooit wys om enigiets vir jou ouers weg te steek nie. Hulle moet weet van daardie verkeerde dinge wat jy doen, maak nie saak hoe verleë of geskuldig jy mag voel nie. Ouers moet weet van alles wat met hulle kinders gebeur. Dit is God se ontwerp dat vaders en moeders daar moet wees vir hulle kinders, om jou te help wanneer jy seerkry, en om jou te lei en te leer terwyl jy leer hoe om goeie, gehoorsame kinders te wees. God se weg is altyd die beste.

De lunch was voorbij en het was dat heerlijke uur van de dag waarop mama zei dat het tijd was voor een pauze. Omdat Ellie tien was, hoefde ze niet meer elke dag een middagdutje te doen, dus begon ze zich te bedenken hoe ze deze vrije tijd zou besteden. Ze hield van buiten zijn, dus de zonnige lucht en de frisse lucht van deze bijzonder mooie zomerdag trokken haar haast naar buiten.

“Ik weet het!” dacht ze bij zichzelf. “Dit is een perfecte gelegenheid om te proberen te snijden met dat mes dat Paul me gegeven heeft.”

Ze had een week bij haar tante en oom doorgebracht die enkele graafschappen verderop woonden, en daar had haar neef Paul haar een mes gegeven dat hij gemaakt had. Het had een kort, rond handvat en hij had een klein stuk staal in één uiteinde geplaatst. Daarna sneed hij het lemmet tot een mooie scherpe rand. Hij kon de grappigste gezichtjes snijden in kleine blokjes hout en Ellie was altijd benieuwd wat hij de volgende keer zou maken. Ze probeerde hem na te doen, maar het leek erop dat ze op korte termijn niets bijzonders zou voortbrengen. Toch was het leuk om te proberen, dus haalde ze het mes uit haar lade in haar slaapkamer en ging naar buiten.

De grote esdoornboom voor hun oude stenen boerderij lonkte naar haar. De laag hangende takken leken de perfecte plek om te zitten en het mes nog eens uit te proberen. Ellie koos een paar grote twijgen en hijste zich vervolgens in de koele schaduw van de boom. Toen ze eenmaal zat, begon ze te snijden en stukjes hout weg te halen. Ze kon nog steeds geen ogen en neus tevoorschijn toveren, maar ze vond het leuk om inkepingen te maken en kleine stukjes schors af te schaven. Het was een ontspannende bezigheid terwijl ze genoot van de stilte van de middag. Ze was zo blij dat deze boom in hun tuin stond, en ze was zo blij dat Paul haar dat snijmes had gegeven.

Na een tijdje begon de tak waarop Ellie zat ruw en hard aan te voelen, en de twijgen die ze aan het snijden was waren bijna verdwenen. “Ik moet even gaan kijken wat de jongens doen,” dacht ze. Ze verplaatste zich naar de laagste tak en zat klaar, gereed om omlaag te springen zoals ze altijd deed om uit de boom te komen.

Ze pauzeerde en keek naar het mes in haar hand. “Spring nooit ergens vanaf terwijl je een mes in je hand houdt!” galmde de stem van haar moeder in haar geheugen. “Dat is heel gevaarlijk. Je kunt jezelf ernstig snijden.” Ellie bleef even nadenken.

“Ja, ik weet dat dat waarschijnlijk waar is,” zei ze tegen zichzelf. “Maar ik denk dat als ik heel voorzichtig ben, ik kan springen en het zal goed gaan,” beredeneerde ze.

Ze klemde het mes stevig in haar rechterhand en sprong toen snel de afstand naar de grond. Net toen ze landde, draaide haar enkel om en knakte naar beneden. Ze viel onhandig op haar linkerbeen. En, o nee! Dat kleine mesje was in haar linkerpols gedrukt terwijl ze probeerde haar evenwicht te bewaren. Snel trok ze het eruit en keek, met haar hart dat snel klopte, hoe het bloed opwelde, donker en warm. Het was een kleine snijwond, slechts ongeveer een kwart inch lang, maar hij was behoorlijk diep.

Wat moest ze nu doen? Ja, daar was geen twijfel over, haar moeder had toch gelijk gehad! In haar hart wist ze dat het juiste zou zijn om meteen naar haar moeder te gaan en te vertellen wat ze had gedaan. Maar ze voelde zich schuldig en beschaamd. Ze had beter moeten weten dan van de tak te springen met dat mes, en toch had ze het gedaan. Schuldig drukte ze snel haar duim op de wond en sloop het huis binnen. Het bloeden stopte al snel, en nadat ze een klein pleistertje had gevonden en dat op haar snee had geplakt, deed ze stilletjes haar mes weg en zocht een boek om te lezen. Ze heeft haar moeder pas veel jaren later, toen ze volwassen was, verteld wat er gebeurd was.

Vandaag, als ze naar die litteken kijkt dat nog steeds zichtbaar is van 40 jaar geleden, vraagt ze zich af waarom God haar beschermd heeft. Ze was een dwaas meisje geweest om niet meteen naar haar moeder te gaan en te belijden wat ze gedaan had. Ze had een ernstige infectie kunnen krijgen van het snijden met een vies, licht roestig mes. Hoewel ze dwaas had gehandeld, is ze dankbaar dat God haar beschermde, maar ze wenst nog steeds dat ze haar ongehoorzaamheid aan haar moeder had beleden.

Het is nooit verstandig om iets voor je ouders te verbergen. Ze moeten weten van die verkeerde dingen die je doet, hoe beschaamd of schaamtevol je je ook kunt voelen. Ouders moeten weten wat er met hun kinderen gebeurt. Het is Gods ontwerp dat vaders en moeders er voor hun kinderen zijn, om je te helpen wanneer je gewond raakt, en om je te begeleiden en te onderwijzen terwijl je leert hoe je goede, gehoorzame kinderen kunt zijn. Gods weg is altijd het beste.

Jehoshaphat was in trouble. He had just heard the news that a great multitude was coming to fight against him. At that moment he did what all of us naturally do when a multitude of problems come against us. He was afraid. How well I know the feeling of fear, the dread that grips my heart at times. Sometimes it’s the big things, like being misunderstood and misused, or the fear and pain of sickness, or the death of a loved one. Sometimes it’s small things, like loneliness on a Sunday afternoon. This is not comfortable, God, and I’m afraid.

Jehoshaphat laid his fear aside, set himself to seek the Lord, and proclaimed a fast throughout all the land of Judah – verse 3. Even in this seemingly impossible situation of having thousands of men on their way to destroy him and his people, he fell before the Lord and acknowledged His perfect, omnipotent rule. And [he] said, O LORD God of our fathers, art not thou God in heaven? and rulest not thou over all the kingdoms of the heathen? and in thine hand is there not power and might, so that none is able to withstand thee? –verse 6.

The choice is mine. I wrestle with my own fearful thoughts, turning them over and over in my mind as if hoping to change the situation with my messy and fearful concoctions. Clinging to my fear gives me a feeling of being in control. But it is killing me from the inside out, even without the dreaded “what ifs” becoming reality. Finally, I let go and fall exhausted at my Lord’s feet, and my heart echoes the words of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah.

In humble entreaty, Jehoshaphat acknowledges their weakness and need for God’s power. O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee. –verse 12.

Yes, God, I am nothing in the grand scheme of things. I have no power, not even to be the fruitful worker in Your kingdom that I always dreamed of being. I can’t fight this battle.

Jehoshaphat realized that he alone, as one man, had no strength. He called all the people of Judah together, And all Judah stood before the LORD, with their little ones, their wives, and their children –verse 13. They knew the strength in unity. As they stood before the Lord, waiting for Him to speak, the Spirit of the Lord came down and God gave them the words of help and hope that they were desperate for.

…Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s –verse 15. Often I try to fight my battles inside of myself rather than making myself vulnerable to others. But, as soon as I invite others into my life and into my battles, I find the strength of God through His people. When we are confused and disillusioned, we need the people of God. When we all pray together, we will get an answer to our prayer for direction.

Jehoshaphat heard the next directive from God. Tomorrow go ye down against them … Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD … fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you –verses 16-17. These words comfort my heart. Often the easiest thing to do is try to fix things, to quickly come up with a remedy of some sort to get myself out of this dilemma, to try to convince myself that everything will be okay. But God tells my heart to sit still without fear and let Him do the fighting. This takes more spiritual muscle than all the action, all the doing, and all the worrying; plus, it accomplishes a lot more.

And Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground: and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell before the LORD, worshipping the LORD –verse 18. If I obey and trust instead of worry and sit still instead of jumping into the middle of things, then I will see God do miracles. No, not always in changing my circumstances or removing all the hard things, but He does a miracle in my own soul which changes my focus and attitude. And that causes me to worship because it’s a miracle which only the all-mighty, all-powerful God can do.

Do you think any of them slept that night? They knew a fearsome army was on its way to destroy them and yet… they had heard God speak. Just perhaps there was a joyful expectation in their hearts and an eager anticipation to see how God was going to win this battle. When I learn to practice trust in the little things and the big things that pile into my life, I will soon learn to have a heart of excited expectation, because I know He is going to do something! He is going to give me a way out. Even if the worst happens, He will show my heart the way of peace and He has promised to be with me through it all. And after all, the ultimate victory is already won, so what do all these infractions really have to do with my peace and joy? Nothing.

Morning dawned; it was the day God had told them to go out against these enemies. They arose with no delay. They all knew obedience was paramount in receiving God’s blessing that day. And as they went out of the city, Jehoshaphat exhorted them. And they rose early in the morning, …and as they went forth, Jehoshaphat stood and said, …Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established; believe his prophets, so shall ye prosper. And… he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army… – verses 21-20. He appointed singers to sing as they went, proclaiming to everyone and to the opposing army that they were on the Lord’s side.

I would have liked to see that huge army going out of the city, singing. They were facing a daunting task and one that would have made the strongest man tremble, but they were singing. And when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set… [an ambush] against the children of Ammon, [and] Moab, …which were come against Judah; and they were smitten …every one helped to destroy another –verses 22-23.

The people of Judah went to their watch tower and in amazement saw that their enemies had destroyed each other, and they saw nothing but an army of dead bodies. When a fearsome battle is set in array against me, I can still make the decision to trust and sing. Singing is a deliberate act of worship; it reminds our own souls and the souls of everyone listening that the Lord, He is God. He is the One in complete charge of my circumstances, of my tiny world, and all its problems. Suddenly the enemies are dead. The circumstances may not have changed, but the battle is finished in my soul.

The army of Judah spent the next three days gathering the riches and spoils from the dead bodies of their enemies, collecting so much that they couldn’t carry it all away with them. Astonishing! But that is how it is every time. My spirit benefits from the hard things that I endure successfully. Each victory allows me to collect ‘spoils’ which will profit me for the rest of my life. My heart is full of blessing, of being cared for, and being carried by a Heavenly Father. The “armies of Moab and Ammon” have brought blessing instead of ruin.

They came again to their homes in Jerusalem with singing, and harps, and trumpets, overloaded with all their spoil. The fear of God fell on all the kingdoms of the land when they heard how God had fought this huge battle, then Jehoshaphat’s realm was quiet. Peace reigned.

The peace of knowing that all I really need is God and His working in my life is the ultimate peace. This broken world can bring all manner of pain, sickness, and disappointments, but God brings rest to the heart that was once so full of tumult and fear. There is rest ‘round about’ and all the ‘kingdoms of the land’ will be amazed and curious at the strength that is within us, because it is the strength that no one can match—the strength of our amazing God.

Joschafat war in Bedrängnis. Er hatte gerade die Nachricht erhalten, dass eine große Schar im Anmarsch sei, um gegen ihn zu kämpfen. In diesem Augenblick tat er das, was wir alle von Natur aus tun, wenn uns eine Vielzahl von Problemen entgegentritt. Er fürchtete sich. Wie gut kenne ich das Gefühl der Furcht, das Entsetzen, das manchmal mein Herz ergreift. Manchmal sind es die großen Dinge, wie missverstanden und ausgenutzt zu werden, oder die Angst und der Schmerz von Krankheit, oder der Tod eines Geliebten. Manchmal sind es kleine Dinge, wie Einsamkeit an einem Sonntagnachmittag. Das ist nicht angenehm, Gott, und ich habe Angst.

Joschafat legte seine Furcht beiseite, machte sich daran, den Herrn zu suchen, und rief im ganzen Land Juda eine Fastenzeit aus – Vers 3. Sogar in dieser scheinbar aussichtslosen Situation, in der Tausende von Männern auf dem Weg waren, ihn und sein Volk zu vernichten, fiel er vor dem Herrn nieder und erkannte Seine vollkommene, allmächtige Herrschaft an. Und er sprach: HERR, Gott unserer Väter, bist du nicht der Gott im Himmel? Herrschst du nicht über alle Reiche der Heiden? Und ist nicht in deiner Hand Macht und Stärke, so daß niemand dir widerstehen kann? – Vers 6.

Die Wahl liegt bei mir. Ich ringe mit meinen eigenen ängstlichen Gedanken, wälze sie immer wieder in meinem Geist, als hoffte ich, die Lage mit meinen wirren und furchtsamen Einfällen verändern zu können. An der Angst festzuhalten gibt mir das Gefühl, die Kontrolle zu haben. Aber es tötet mich von innen her, noch bevor die gefürchteten „Was wäre wenn“-Szenarien Wirklichkeit werden. Schließlich lasse ich los und falle erschöpft zu den Füßen meines Herrn, und mein Herz hallt die Worte Joschafats, des Königs von Juda, wider.

In demütiger Bitte anerkennt Joschafat ihre Schwäche und das Bedürfnis nach Gottes Macht. O unser Gott, willst du sie nicht richten? Denn wir haben keine Kraft gegen diese große Schar, die gegen uns kommt; und wir wissen nicht, was wir tun sollen; aber unsere Augen sind auf dich gerichtet. – Vers 12.

Ja, Gott, ich bin nichts im großen Gefüge der Dinge. Ich habe keine Macht, nicht einmal, der fruchtbare Arbeiter in Deinem Reich zu sein, der ich immer zu sein träumte. Ich kann diesen Kampf nicht kämpfen.

Joschafat begriff, dass er allein, als einzelner Mann, keine Stärke hatte. Er rief das ganze Volk Juda zusammen, Und ganz Juda stand vor dem HERRN, samt ihren Kleinen, ihren Frauen und ihren Kindern – Vers 13. Sie kannten die Stärke der Einheit. Als sie vor dem Herrn standen und darauf warteten, dass Er sprach, kam der Geist des Herrn auf sie herab, und Gott gab ihnen die Worte der Hilfe und Hoffnung, nach denen sie sich gesehnt hatten.

…Seid nicht verzagt und erschreckt wegen dieser großen Schar; denn der Kampf ist nicht euer, sondern Gottes – Vers 15. Oft versuche ich, meine Kämpfe in mir selbst zu führen, anstatt mich anderen gegenüber verletzlich zu machen. Aber sobald ich andere in mein Leben und in meine Kämpfe einlade, finde ich durch Sein Volk die Stärke Gottes. Wenn wir verwirrt und enttäuscht sind, brauchen wir die Menschen Gottes. Wenn wir alle gemeinsam beten, erhalten wir eine Antwort auf unser Gebet um Wegweisung.

Joschafat hörte die nächste Anweisung von Gott. Geht morgen gegen sie hinab … Ihr werdet in diesem Kampf nicht kämpfen müssen: stellt euch hin, bleibt stehen und seht die Errettung des HERRN … fürchtet euch nicht und erschreckt nicht; morgen zieht aus gegen sie; denn der HERR ist mit euch – Verse 16–17. Diese Worte trösten mein Herz. Oft ist das Einfachste, Dinge zu beheben, schnell irgendein Mittel zu finden, um mich aus diesem Dilemma zu befreien, zu versuchen, mich selbst davon zu überzeugen, dass alles gut werden wird. Aber Gott sagt meinem Herzen, ruhig zu bleiben ohne Furcht und Ihn den Kampf führen zu lassen. Das erfordert mehr geistliche Kraft als all das Handeln, Tun und Sorgen; und außerdem bewirkt es viel mehr.

Und Joschafat beugte sein Haupt mit dem Angesicht zur Erde; und ganz Juda und die Einwohner Jerusalems fielen vor dem HERRN nieder und beteten den HERRN an – Vers 18. Wenn ich gehorche und vertraue, statt mich zu sorgen, und still halte, statt mich mitten hineinzuwerfen, werde ich sehen, wie Gott Wunder tut. Nein, nicht immer, indem Er meine Umstände ändert oder alle harten Dinge entfernt, aber Er wirkt ein Wunder in meiner eigenen Seele, das meinen Fokus und meine Haltung verändert. Und das veranlasst mich zum Lobpreis, weil es ein Wunder ist, das nur der allmächtige, allherrliche Gott tun kann.

Glaubst du, dass einer von ihnen in jener Nacht geschlafen hat? Sie wussten, dass eine furchtbare Armee im Anmarsch war, ihnen Verderben zu bringen, und dennoch … sie hatten Gott reden hören. Vielleicht war da eine freudige Erwartung in ihren Herzen und eine eifrige Vorfreude darauf, zu sehen, wie Gott diesen Kampf gewinnen würde. Wenn ich lerne, Vertrauen in den kleinen Dingen und den großen Dingen zu üben, die sich in mein Leben auftürmen, werde ich bald ein Herz voller erwarteter Freude haben, weil ich weiß, dass Er etwas tun wird! Er wird mir einen Ausweg geben. Selbst wenn das Schlimmste geschieht, wird Er meinem Herzen den Weg des Friedens zeigen, und Er hat versprochen, mit mir durch alles hindurch zu sein. Und schließlich ist der endgültige Sieg bereits errungen, also was haben all diese Verstöße wirklich mit meinem Frieden und meiner Freude zu tun? Nichts.

Der Morgen dämmerte; es war der Tag, an dem Gott ihnen gesagt hatte, gegen diese Feinde auszuziehen. Sie standen ohne Verzögerung auf. Sie alle wussten, dass Gehorsam an diesem Tag entscheidend war, um Gottes Segen zu empfangen. Und als sie aus der Stadt gingen, ermahnte Joschafat sie. Und sie standen früh am Morgen auf, …und da sie hinauszogen, stand Joschafat auf und sprach, …Glaubt an den HERRN, euren Gott, so werdet ihr fest bestehen; glaubt seinen Propheten, so wird es euch wohl ergehen. Und … er setzte Sänger vor dem HERRN, die die Schönheit der Heiligkeit loben sollten, während sie vor dem Heer hergingen… – verses 21-20. Er setzte Sänger ein, die beim Auszug sangen und damit allen und der feindlichen Schar verkündeten, dass sie auf der Seite des Herrn standen.

Ich hätte gern die große Armee gesehen, wie sie singend aus der Stadt zog. Sie standen vor einer gewaltigen Aufgabe, die den stärksten Mann erzittern lassen hätte, doch sie sangen. Und als sie zu singen und zu loben anfingen, stellte der HERR einen Hinterhalt gegen die Kinder Ammon und Moab … die gegen Juda gekommen waren; und sie wurden geschlagen … ein jeder half dem andern, sie umzubringen – Verse 22–23.

Das Volk Judas ging zu seinem Wachturm und sah staunend, dass ihre Feinde einander vernichtet hatten; sie sahen nichts als ein Heer toter Leiber. Wenn sich eine furchtbare Schlacht gegen mich aufstellt, kann ich dennoch die Entscheidung treffen, zu vertrauen und zu singen. Singen ist eine bewusste Tat des Gottesdienstes; es erinnert unsere eigene Seele und die Seelen aller Zuhörenden daran, dass der Herr der ist, der Gott ist. Er ist derjenige, der vollkommen über meine Umstände herrscht, über meine kleine Welt und all ihre Probleme. Plötzlich sind die Feinde tot. Die Umstände mögen sich nicht verändert haben, aber der Kampf ist in meiner Seele beendet.

Die Armee Judas verbrachte die nächsten drei Tage damit, den Reichtum und die Beute von den toten Leibern ihrer Feinde zu sammeln, so viel, dass sie es nicht alles forttragen konnten. Erstaunlich! Aber so ist es jedes Mal. Mein Geist profitiert von den schweren Dingen, die ich erfolgreich durchstehe. Jeder Sieg ermöglicht mir, „Beute“ zu sammeln, die mir für den Rest meines Lebens zugutekommt. Mein Herz ist voll Segen, voller Fürsorge und getragen von einem himmlischen Vater. Die „Heere von Moab und Ammon“ haben Segen gebracht statt Verderben.

Sie kamen singend, mit Harfen und Trompeten, überladen mit aller Beute, wieder in ihre Häuser in Jerusalem. Die Furcht vor Gott fiel auf alle Reiche des Landes, als sie hörten, wie Gott diesen großen Kampf geführt hatte; dann war das Reich Joschafats ruhig. Frieden herrschte.

Der Friede zu wissen, dass alles, was ich wirklich brauche, Gott ist und Sein Wirken in meinem Leben, ist der höchste Friede. Diese zerbrochene Welt kann allerlei Schmerz, Krankheit und Enttäuschungen bringen, aber Gott bringt Ruhe dem Herzen, das einst so voll Aufruhr und Furcht war. Es gibt Ruhe „ringsumher“ und alle „Reiche des Landes“ werden erstaunt und neugierig sein über die Kraft, die in uns liegt, denn es ist die Kraft, die niemand übertreffen kann – die Kraft unseres wunderbaren Gottes.

For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect. For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. …it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe –1 Corinthians –1:17-21.

The modern Christian world has duly accepted many of the lowly vehicles that God used to usher in the Kingdom. The virgin birth, the rough-hewn manger, and the swaddling clothes have become sovereign monuments that we could scarcely do without. Even the rude donkey is appreciated on Good Friday and the old, rugged cross has become a spiritual emblem nominally displayed on neck chains and ornate pulpit carvings. While man remains infatuated with the traditional symbols of the gospel, there remains an absurd avenue of God’s choosing that is becoming increasingly despised.

For centuries, the Gospel was heralded by foolish and unlearned men (according to their elite and intellectual counterparts). The biblical truth spoken in simplicity was sufficient of itself for God’s Holy Spirit to use to convert the sinner. While there is no lack for preaching in these days, it appears that much of it is of a different sort than the original form that Christ exemplified. If anyone was capable of articulating a flourish of orations in an accurate philosophical language it would have been the Apostle Paul. Yet, he refused to preach the gospel in this manner, …lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect –1 Corinthians 1:17. He preached carefully, lest the success should be ascribed to the force of art, and not of truth itself.

Paul had been ingrained in Jewish learning at the feet of Gamaliel and was affluent in understanding both Hebrew and Greek, but in preaching the cross of Christ, he laid his learning aside. He spoke the words of the Gospel in a language void of human power lest the honor belonging to Christ be eclipsed by his own personal power. For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible –2 Corinthians 10:10. It is here where the modern church has spurned the meager vehicles chosen by Christ and the Apostles while diverting to a route more acceptable to in our day. Modern day efficiency demands a more direct route to the end, and if the Bible doesn’t forbid it, we feel that it is our prerogative to employ it.

While evangelical films, music concerts, and a host of other questionable venues of ministry could be mentioned, I wish to speak primarily to the modern invitation system known as the “altar call”. While it is commonly associated with the “old fashioned meetings” of the past two centuries, it is indeed modern due to the fact that for nearly nineteen centuries no one had ever heard of the practice. Evangelists such as George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards, and even John Wesley had never heard of such a custom. Even Charles Spurgeon (heralded as the “Prince of Preachers”) strongly criticized it and refused to adopt it.*

Thus, we observe, the practice was not born in the apostolic church. It is not found in the ministry of Jesus, His apostles, or even the church of the post-apostolic period. We do see Jesus and the apostles inviting men and women to come to Christ and to be saved, but never by means of this particular method. So why has this practice become such an essential tool in most evangelical and in many Anabaptist churches today? The answer—pragmatic results. Immediately following the sermon, the congregation will sing a hymn during which the preacher calls men and women to walk to the front of the auditorium (to the “altar”) to make a public decision for Christ. Salvation is offered to all who will but come to the front and receive it. Those who come often receive the personal attention of a counselor to pray with them and lead them through confession.

This practice was designed to encourage decisions and obtain results. So, it did. And with slight variations the new method spread with increasing popularity through Charles Finney, and later, Dwight L. Moody, and finally, into virtually all of nineteenth and twentieth century evangelicalism. Peter Cartwright, Sam Jones, R. A. Torrey, Billy Sunday, Bob Jones, Gipsy Smith, John R. Rice, Billy Graham, and George Brunk all employed the method with impressive success. Thus, the invitation system became the accepted normal practice and those who question it are often deemed spiritually eccentric.

Why should we take issue with the practice if the scripture doesn’t forbid it? The answer lies in the question of the propriety of the invitation system. Let us first note that the Scriptures abound with invitations to salvation. Such offers as, Come unto me, …and I will give you rest –Matthew 11:28, and, …If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink –John 7:37, are marvelous offers of life to those who will trust Christ. The apostles also did not hesitate to show forth Christ as Savior to all who would listen to their message.

They preached indiscriminately, Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out… –Acts 3:19, and …we pray you in Christ›s stead, be ye reconciled to God –2 Corinthians 5:20. And they testified …to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ –Acts 20:21. With all this, every Christian should not only agree but also rejoice.

Finally, …compel them to come in, that my house may be filled –Luke 14:23, is another Bible verse which could be used to lend support to the altar call method. Still, this says nothing to bolster the correctness of the altar call. As we examine the practice at its roots, we cannot help but observe a few deficiencies:

…Extra-Biblical

This is no reflection upon the multitudes who have found salvation at such an event. The angels in heaven rejoice at the repentance of every sinner no matter how he arrives there. We simply wish to hold forth the simplicity of the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe. The altar call is used as a specific addition to the sermon to bring to fruition what the foolishness of preaching itself could not do.

The altar call gained popularity in the 1830’s with the preaching of Charles G. Finney who wrote, “A revival is not a miracle, or dependent on a miracle, in any sense. It is a purely philosophical result of the right use of the constituted means.” ** We cannot accuse all who practice the altar call of believing this, but it is rather revealing that the preacher who brought it to popularity seemed to liken it more to a mathematical equation than to divine involvement.

When the truth falls on the soil of a good and honest heart, the seed veritably takes root and produces fruit. This seed of truth needs no artificial dress. It shines out with the greatest majesty in its own light and prevails in the world by its divine authority. It is a demonstration of the Spirit, without need of human invention or intervention. The plain preaching of a crucified Christ is more powerful than all the oratory, philosophical, and heart gripping modes of the world.

…Emotional Thrust

The altar call requires a seeker to leave his seat and walk to the forefront for pardon. These invitations are often preceded by fearfully moving accounts, sad stories, or testimonies that stir the emotions to fear, guilt, or regret. Flanked by a soft hymn sung by the congregation, the emotions are ripe to move forward. Those who choose to repent from their seat without responding are often esteemed as “missing an opportunity”.

And these are they likewise which are sown on stony ground; who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness; And have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word’s sake, immediately they are offended –Mark 4:16-17. We refuse to deduce that all who were converted under this type of ministry are stony ground hearers. Yet, the vast majority of those who receive it in such a charged emotional environment will often have a less than sincere conversion.

I once had an exuberant client in my shop who informed me that their church had sponsored a national evangelical ministry to preach at the public high school. “There were over 400 decisions for Christ!” While we all wish to rejoice with the angels, one cannot but question how many of them were still in church a year later. While the lack of true commitment may not fall upon the use of the altar call alone, we may be sure that the seed so quick to spring up will surely manifest itself at the moorings of an emotional invitation. Those that have no root would be better off never having responded prematurely.

Conversions wrought through emotional channels are often questionable and transient. Holy Spirit promptings do not need human strength, wisdom, or efforts to convey them forth. Revival methods such as shouting, overt weeping, emotion eliciting music, and the telling of sentimental stories is the man-made art of preaching. It is also found in many other public venues that are designed to elicit a specific predetermined response from the hearer. Each of these dimensions is quite natural to human behavior and, at times, there may be a fine line between what is acceptable and unacceptable in preaching. Great care should be taken that we do not create an emotional climax and eclipse the message in an inordinate manner lest the power be of men and not of Christ.

…Encroachment to Parental and Local Church Authority

Children are often a target at such a time. They may feel guilty for some childish misdeed, but a fiery message followed by emotional pleading can be very unsettling. These are times when a parent should speak to the heart of their child and connect in a spiritual way. Instead, often the child is moved to the front and given a church counselor for them to pour out their confession.

I know a woman whose father was an itinerant evangelical preacher. She claims that she responded “hundreds of times” to the altar call. A casual and honest appraisal would reveal that while the altar call may bring commencement to many sincere conversions, it also avails itself equally to a host of premature decisions and pressure-driven commitments. This often leaves many unstable souls wallowing in spiritual instability and struggling with a lack of assurance of salvation for years to come.

For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel. Wherefore I beseech you, be ye followers of me –1 Corinthians 4:15-16. God has ordained fathers and mothers to bring birth to their children, both physical and spiritual.

Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ –1 Corinthians 11:1. The skilled itinerant evangelist has no intention of begetting spiritual children and making followers of himself. This he leaves to others, for he has found his gift in compelling people to make decisions.

And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you; And to esteem them very highly in love for their work’s sake… –1 Thessalonians 5:13. But there is to be a God-given loyalty to those spiritual fathers who labor over us and bring us to birth beyond the many instructors upon life’s pathway. The contemporary emergence of thousands of “hit and run” ministries should cause us concern.

While public confession of sin is obviously an important doctrine of Christ to accompany salvation, these confessions belong in the hands of the spiritual authorities who can discern the situation and help further the soul through tomorrow’s temptations. When those who know the convert are personally engaged, a more thorough and honest examination can be employed to bring about a sincere conversion. This will lay the groundwork for the deep digging required to lay the foundation upon the Rock and establish the soul, both in the home and in the church.

…Engineered Faith

When people are continually subject to revival scenes, there is often an unspoken expectation that the meetings are the place to do business with God. This has a tendency to confuse “saving faith” with a “saving act”. The emphasis on “coming forward to receive Christ” confuses the meaning of faith. Christ is the strong consolation, to whom we … have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast… –Hebrews 6:18-19.(emphasis mine)

The invitation of Christ to …Come unto me… Matthew 11:28, should never be confused with “coming to the altar” (walking to the front). The foolishness of preaching is the invitation, and “Christ” is the destination. The power of the oration shall not lie in the dynamics of the preacher but within the truth of the message. We become like paper figures, having no power at all in ourselves. All power must come from above; all methods used must also come from above. –Watchman Nee ***

The wind bloweth where it listeth… John 3:8, likewise the Holy Spirit, and the preacher must be content with that. I trust that many who give altar calls have the best of intentions and do not wish to circumvent the Spirit. But most works accomplished in the apex of emotion have a strong inclination to be fallacious. So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God –Romans 10:17.

Endnotes:

* “Charles Spurgeon, well known for his evangelistic abilities, firmly refused to adopt the practice of altar calls and he severely criticized it. He viewed the altar call as a method to force decisions as results, but he recognized its potential abuse and dangers.” Altar Calls – Bill Brenner

** What A Revival Of Religion Is – Charles Grandison Finney – The Belknap Press Of Harvard University A “Revival of Religion” presupposes a declension. Almost all the religion in the world has been produced by revivals. God has found it necessary to take advantage of the excitability there is in mankind, to produce powerful excitements among them, before he can lead them to obey. Men are so sluggish, there are so many things to lead their minds off from religion, and to oppose the influence of the gospel that it is necessary to raise an excitement among them, till the tide rises so high as to sweep away the opposing obstacles. They must be so excited that they will break over these counteracting influences, before they will obey God.

*** Spirit Force vs. Psychic Force – Watchman Nee

Porque Cristo no me envió a bautizar, sino a predicar el evangelio; no con sabiduría de palabras, para que no se haga vana la cruz de Cristo. Porque la predicación de la cruz es locura para los que se pierden; pero para los que se salvan, para nosotros, es poder de Dios. …a Dios le plació salvar a los creyentes por la necedad de la predicación –1 Corintios –1:17-21.

El mundo cristiano moderno ha aceptado debidamente muchos de los humildes vehículos que Dios usó para introducir el Reino. El nacimiento virginal, el pesebre toscamente tallado y las mantas para envolver al niño se han convertido en monumentos soberanos de los que apenas podríamos prescindir. Incluso el rústico burro es apreciado el Viernes Santo y la vieja y áspera cruz se ha convertido en un emblema espiritual que se exhibe nominalmente en cadenas para el cuello y tallas ornamentales en púlpitos. Mientras el hombre continúa enamorado de los símbolos tradicionales del evangelio, permanece una vía absurda escogida por Dios que cada vez es más despreciada.

Durante siglos, el Evangelio fue proclamado por hombres necios e iletrados (según sus contrapartes élite e intelectuales). La verdad bíblica dicha con simplicidad fue suficiente por sí misma para que el Espíritu Santo de Dios la usara para convertir al pecador. Si bien hoy no falta predicación, parece que gran parte de ella es de un tipo distinto al formato original que Cristo ejemplificó. Si alguien hubiera sido capaz de articular un floreo de oratoria en un lenguaje filosófico preciso, habría sido el apóstol Pablo. Sin embargo, se negó a predicar el evangelio de esa manera, …para que no se haga vana la cruz de Cristo –1 Corintios 1:17. Predicó con cuidado, para que el éxito no se atribuyera a la fuerza del arte, y no a la verdad misma.

Pablo había sido formado en el aprendizaje judío a los pies de Gamaliel y dominaba tanto el hebreo como el griego, pero al predicar la cruz de Cristo, dejó de lado su erudición. Pronunció las palabras del Evangelio en un lenguaje desprovisto de poder humano, para que la honra perteneciente a Cristo no quedara eclipsada por su propio poder personal. Porque dicen sus cartas que son ponderosas y fuertes; pero su presencia corporal es débil, y su palabra despreciable –2 Corintios 10:10. Es aquí donde la iglesia moderna ha desdeñado los escasos vehículos escogidos por Cristo y los apóstoles, desviándose hacia una ruta más aceptable en nuestros días. La eficiencia contemporánea exige una ruta más directa al fin, y si la Biblia no la prohíbe, sentimos que es nuestra prerrogativa emplearla.

Si bien podrían mencionarse películas evangélicas, conciertos de música y una serie de otros escenarios cuestionables de ministerio, deseo hablar principalmente del sistema moderno de invitación conocido como el “llamado al altar”. Aunque comúnmente se asocia con las “reuniones a la antigua” de los últimos dos siglos, es en realidad moderno debido a que durante casi diecinueve siglos nadie había oído hablar de la práctica. Evangelistas como George Whitefield, Jonathan Edwards e incluso John Wesley nunca habían oído hablar de tal costumbre. Incluso Charles Spurgeon (venerado como el “Príncipe de los Predicadores”) la criticó con severidad y se negó a adoptarla.*

Así, observamos que la práctica no nació en la iglesia apostólica. No se encuentra en el ministerio de Jesús, sus apóstoles, ni siquiera en la iglesia del periodo post-apostólico. Vemos a Jesús y a los apóstoles invitando a hombres y mujeres a venir a Cristo y a ser salvos, pero nunca por medio de este método particular. Entonces, ¿por qué esta práctica se ha vuelto una herramienta tan esencial en la mayoría de las iglesias evangélicas y en muchas anabaptistas hoy en día? La respuesta: resultados pragmáticos. Inmediatamente después del sermón, la congregación canta un himno durante el cual el predicador llama a hombres y mujeres a caminar hacia el frente del auditorio (al “altar”) para tomar una decisión pública por Cristo. La salvación se ofrece a todos los que simplemente vengan al frente y la reciban. Los que vienen a menudo reciben la atención personal de un consejero para orar con ellos y guiarles en la confesión.

Esta práctica fue diseñada para fomentar decisiones y obtener resultados. Y lo hizo. Y con ligeras variaciones, el nuevo método se difundió con creciente popularidad a través de Charles Finney, y más tarde Dwight L. Moody, y finalmente, en prácticamente todo el evangelicalismo de los siglos XIX y XX. Peter Cartwright, Sam Jones, R. A. Torrey, Billy Sunday, Bob Jones, Gipsy Smith, John R. Rice, Billy Graham y George Brunk emplearon todos el método con éxito impresionante. De este modo, el sistema de invitación se convirtió en la práctica normal aceptada y quienes lo cuestionan a menudo son considerados espiritualmente excéntricos.

¿Por qué habríamos de objetar la práctica si la Escritura no la prohíbe? La respuesta reside en la cuestión de la idoneidad (o pertinencia) del sistema de invitación. Notemos primero que las Escrituras abundan en invitaciones a la salvación. Ofertas tales como, Venid a mí... y yo os haré descansar –Mateo 11:28, y, …Si alguno tiene sed, venga a mí y beba –Juan 7:37, son maravillosas ofertas de vida para los que confiarán en Cristo. Los apóstoles tampoco dudaron en mostrar a Cristo como Salvador a todos los que escucharan su mensaje.

Predicaron indiscriminadamente, Arrepentíos, pues, y convertíos, para que sean borrados vuestros pecados… –Hechos 3:19, y …os rogamos en nombre de Cristo, reconciliaos con Dios –2 Corintios 5:20. Y testificaron …a los judíos y también a los griegos, arrepentimiento para con Dios y fe para con nuestro Señor Jesucristo –Hechos 20:21. Con todo esto, todo cristiano no solo debería estar de acuerdo sino también regocijarse.

Finalmente, …forzadlos a entrar, para que se llene mi casa –Lucas 14:23, es otro versículo bíblico que podría usarse para respaldar el método del llamado al altar. Aun así, esto no dice nada que reforzara la corrección del llamado al altar. Al examinar la práctica en sus raíces, no podemos menos que observar algunas deficiencias:

…Extrabíblico

Esto no es un reproche hacia las multitudes que han hallado salvación en tal evento. Los ángeles en el cielo se regocijan por el arrepentimiento de todo pecador sin importar cómo haya llegado allí. Simplemente deseamos sostener la simplicidad de la necedad de la predicación para salvar a los creyentes. El llamado al altar se utiliza como una adición específica al sermón para llevar a buen término aquello que la necedad de la predicación por sí sola no pudo lograr.

El llamado al altar ganó popularidad en la década de 1830 con la predicación de Charles G. Finney, quien escribió: “Un avivamiento no es un milagro, ni depende de un milagro, en ningún sentido. Es un resultado puramente filosófico del uso correcto de los medios constituidos.” ** No podemos acusar a todos los que practican el llamado al altar de creer esto, pero resulta revelador que el predicador que lo popularizó pareciera igualarlo más a una ecuación matemática que a una intervención divina.

Cuando la verdad cae en la tierra de un corazón bueno y honrado, la semilla verdaderamente arraiga y produce fruto. Esta semilla de la verdad no necesita aderezo artificial. Resplandece con la mayor majestad en su propia luz y prevalece en el mundo por su autoridad divina. Es una demostración del Espíritu, sin necesidad de invención o intervención humana. La predicación llana de un Cristo crucificado es más poderosa que toda la oratoria, la filosofía y los modos conmovedores del mundo.

…Impulso emocional

El llamado al altar exige que un buscador deje su asiento y camine al frente para obtener el perdón. Estas invitaciones a menudo van precedidas de relatos profundamente conmovedores, historias tristes o testimonios que agitan las emociones hacia el temor, la culpa o el remordimiento. Flanqueadas por un himno suave cantado por la congregación, las emociones están maduras para avanzar. Aquellos que eligen arrepentirse desde su asiento sin responder suelen ser considerados como “perdiendo una oportunidad”.

Y estos son los que son sembrados sobre la tierra pedregosa; los que, cuando han oído la palabra, la reciben al momento con gozo; y no tienen raíz en sí mismos, sino que duran un tiempo; después que viene la aflicción o la persecución a causa de la palabra, luego se ofenden –Marcos 4:16-17. Nos negamos a deducir que todos los que fueron convertidos bajo este tipo de ministerio sean oidores de tierra pedregosa. Sin embargo, la gran mayoría de los que la reciben en un ambiente emocional tan cargado a menudo tendrán una conversión menos que sincera.

Una vez tuve un cliente entusiasta en mi taller que me informó que su iglesia había patrocinado un ministerio evangelístico nacional para predicar en la escuela secundaria pública. “¡Hubo más de 400 decisiones por Cristo!” Aunque todos deseamos regocijarnos con los ángeles, no se puede menos que cuestionar cuántos de ellos seguían en la iglesia un año después. Si bien la falta de compromiso verdadero puede no recaer únicamente en el uso del llamado al altar, podemos estar seguros de que la semilla tan pronta a brotar sin duda se manifestará en los fondeaderos de una invitación emocional. Los que no tienen raíz habrían hecho mejor en no responder prematuramente.

Las conversiones forjadas por canales emocionales suelen ser dudosas y transitorias. Las inspiraciones del Espíritu Santo no necesitan fuerza, sabiduría o esfuerzos humanos para hacerse presente. Métodos de avivamiento como gritos, llantos manifiestos, música que provoca emoción y el relato de historias sentimentales son el arte hecho por el hombre de predicar. También se encuentran en muchos otros escenarios públicos diseñados para provocar una respuesta predeterminada del oyente. Cada una de estas dimensiones es bastante natural al comportamiento humano y, a veces, puede haber una delgada línea entre lo aceptable y lo inaceptable en la predicación. Debe tenerse gran cuidado para no crear un clímax emocional y eclipsar el mensaje de manera desproporcionada, no sea que el poder sea de los hombres y no de Cristo.

…Invasión de la autoridad parental y de la iglesia local

Los niños suelen ser un objetivo en ese momento. Pueden sentirse culpables por alguna travesura infantil, pero un mensaje encendido seguido de súplicas emotivas puede resultar muy perturbador. Estos son momentos en los que un padre debería hablar al corazón de su hijo y conectarse de forma espiritual. En cambio, a menudo el niño es llevado al frente y se le asigna un consejero de la iglesia para que derrame su confesión.

Conozco a una mujer cuyo padre fue un predicador itinerante evangélico. Ella afirma haber respondido “cientos de veces” al llamado al altar. Una evaluación casual y honesta revelaría que si bien el llamado al altar puede dar inicio a muchas conversiones sinceras, también sirve por igual a una multitud de decisiones prematuras y compromisos producto de la presión. Esto deja a menudo a muchas almas inestables revolcándose en la inestabilidad espiritual y luchando con la falta de seguridad de la salvación durante años.

Pues aunque tengáis diez mil pedagógos en Cristo, no tenéis muchos padres; porque en Cristo Jesús yo os engendré por medio del evangelio. Por tanto os ruego que seáis imitadores de mí –1 Corintios 4:15-16. Dios ha ordenado que haya padres y madres para dar a luz a sus hijos, tanto físicos como espirituales.

Seded imitadores de mí, así como yo de Cristo –1 Corintios 11:1. El hábil evangelista itinerante no tiene intención de engendrar hijos espirituales ni de hacer seguidores de sí mismo. Esto lo deja a otros, pues ha hallado su don en obligar a la gente a tomar decisiones.

Y os rogamos, hermanos, que reconozcáis a los que trabajan entre vosotros, y que os presiden en el Señor, y que os amonestan; y que los tengáis en mucha estima y amor por causa de su obra… –1 Tesalonicenses 5:13. Pero debe haber una lealtad dada por Dios hacia esos padres espirituales que trabajan sobre nosotros y nos traen al nacimiento más allá de los muchos instructores en el camino de la vida. La aparición contemporánea de miles de ministerios de “golpe y huida” debería inquietarnos.

Si bien la confesión pública del pecado es obviamente una doctrina importante de Cristo que acompaña a la salvación, estas confesiones pertenecen a las manos de las autoridades espirituales que pueden discernir la situación y ayudar a avanzar el alma frente a las tentaciones venideras. Cuando aquellos que conocen al convertido se involucran personalmente, puede emplearse un examen más completo y honesto para provocar una conversión sincera. Esto sentará las bases para la profunda excavación requerida para asentar el fundamento sobre la Roca y establecer el alma, tanto en el hogar como en la iglesia.

…Fe diseñada

Cuando las personas están continuamente sujetas a escenas de avivamiento, suele existir una expectativa no expresada de que las reuniones son el lugar para hacer negocios con Dios. Esto tiene tendencia a confundir la “fe salvífica” con un “acto salvador”. El énfasis en “venir al frente para recibir a Cristo” confunde el significado de la fe. Cristo es la fuerte consolación, a quien …hemos acudido para alcanzar la esperanza puesta delante de nosotros; la cual tenemos como un ancla del alma, tanto segura como firme… –Hebreos 6:18-19. (énfasis mío)

La invitación de Cristo a …Venid a mí… Mateo 11:28, nunca debe confundirse con “venir al altar” (caminar al frente). La necedad de la predicación es la invitación, y “Cristo” es el destino. El poder de la oratoria no residirá en la dinámica del predicador sino en la verdad del mensaje. Nos volvemos como figuras de papel, sin tener poder alguno en nosotros. Todo poder debe venir de lo alto; todos los métodos usados también deben venir de lo alto. –Watchman Nee ***

El viento sopla donde quiere… Juan 3:8, así también el Espíritu Santo, y el predicador debe contentarse con ello. Confío en que muchos que hacen llamados al altar tienen las mejores intenciones y no desean eludir al Espíritu. Pero la mayoría de las obras realizadas en el ápice de la emoción tienden a ser falaces. Así que la fe viene por el oír, y el oír por la palabra de Dios –Romanos 10:17.

Notas finales:

* “Charles Spurgeon, bien conocido por sus habilidades evangelísticas, se negó firmemente a adoptar la práctica de los llamados al altar y la criticó severamente. Consideraba el llamado al altar como un método para forzar decisiones como resultados, pero reconocía su potencial de abuso y peligros.” Llamados al Altar – Bill Brenner

‘Me gustaría ir al cuarto de inquirimiento.’ Me imagino que querrías, pero no estamos dispuestos a satisfacer la superstición popular. Tememos que en esos cuartos los hombres se calienten en una confianza ficticia. Muy pocos de los supuestos convertidos de los cuartos de inquirimiento resultan bien. Ve a tu Dios ahora mismo, incluso donde te encuentras. Arroja tu carga sobre Cristo ahora, antes de mover un centímetro!’ - Súplicas y Aliento – Charles Haddon Spurgeon – 17 ago. 1841

** Qué es un avivamiento de la religión – Charles Grandison Finney – The Belknap Press Of Harvard University Un “Avivamiento de la Religión” presupone una decadencia. Casi toda la religión en el mundo ha sido producida por avivamientos. Dios ha considerado necesario aprovechar la excitabilidad que hay en la humanidad, para producir potentes excitaciones entre ellos, antes de que pueda conducirlos a obedecer. Los hombres son tan perezosos, hay tantas cosas que apartan sus mentes de la religión y que se oponen a la influencia del evangelio, que es necesario levantar una excitación entre ellos, hasta que la marea suba tanto que arrase los obstáculos opuestos. Deben estar tan excitados que rompan sobre estas influencias contrarias, antes de que obedezcan a Dios.

*** Fuerza espiritual vs. fuerza psíquica – Watchman Nee

This hymn is generally thought to be one of the most loved hymns written during the latter part of the 19th century. The writing of this thoughtful and beautifully constructed text is even more amazing when we consider that its author was one who was almost completely blind and who describes the writing of this hymn as the “fruit of much mental suffering,” and “the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life.”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, March 27, 1842, George Matheson had only partial vision as a boy, and, after entering Glasgow University, his eyesight continued to fail rapidly. Except for “moments of shadowy eyesight”, he was totally blind by the age of 18. This affliction of blindness seemed to be a tragedy since he was an eager and avid scholar, yet it caused him to trust in the Lord, and it strengthened his walk with God.

He entered the university at the early age of 15 and graduated with high honors in 1861 at the age of 19. He was a brilliant scholar, even spending four more years after graduation in more theological studies, all the while remaining single. After his graduation he became entirely dependent on others, relying much upon his two sisters, who were so dedicated that they learned Latin, Greek, and Hebrew since they thought it might aid him in his theological studies. One of them continued to be his faithful co-worker and helper throughout his life, assisting in his calling of being a pastor and other ministerial duties.

After completing his theological course, he became assistant pastor to the renowned Dr. Macduff, in whose church of thousands of members he had been brought up. Soon, however, he was chosen minister of the Church of Scotland in the seaport summer resort of Innellan. Here he stayed for eighteen years. Many families came to spend the summer there chiefly to be inspired by his preaching ministry.

Whenever he preached, the open Bible was before him as he stood in the pulpit, and to the congregation, he seemed to be reading from it. During the messages, his eyes looked straight at the congregation, and many went away with no clue that they just listened to a blind preacher. It was during this time that he made a practice of memorizing his sermons, as well as the passages of Scripture he used in his messages. His memory was so sharp that if someone read one of his prepared sermons to him twice, or whatever else he wanted to memorize, he could from then on repeat it perfectly. One Sunday, however, after doing this for 12 years, when in the middle of a powerful sermon his memory completely collapsed, and the topic on which he was preaching vanished from his mind. He sat down and commenced to request a psalm to be sung, and, after the song, with perfect calmness told the audience what had happened. With this done, he stood to his feet, gave out a new text, and preached an impromptu sermon of great power. After that experience George wrote little of his sermons, and finally prepared only an outline from which to preach.

Dr. Matheson’s final pastorate was taken up in 1886 at the age of 44 where he became pastor of the large St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, where his eloquent preaching consistently attracted large throngs of people to the services. Here he remained for 13 years, his church growing from 1,494 members to 1,703 in the first 5 years. He continued faithfully preaching the gospel and became well known as one of Scotland’s outstanding preachers and pastors and was greatly esteemed in Edinburgh where he resided.

Many speculations have been made regarding the cause of the mental distress which prompted the author to write this text. A very popular account, although never verified, is that this text was a result of the severe trial Matheson faced after his soon-to-be bride left him just before their marriage when she learned of his impending total blindness. Although this story cannot be documented, there are many significant hints in this hymn reflecting a saddened heart, such as the “flickering torch” and the “borrowed ray” in the second verse, the tracing of the “rainbow through the rain” in the third stanza, as well as the “cross” in the last verse.

Fortunately, Dr. Matheson did relate an account of his writing of this hymn:

“My hymn was composed in the manse of Innellan on the evening of June 6, 1882. I was at that time alone. It was the day of my sister’s wedding, and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow. Something happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering and was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. A genuine inspiration, I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes and equally sure it never received at my hands any retouching or correction. I have no natural gift of rhythm. All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

Treasury of Hymn Stories

Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

Hierdie gesang word algemeen beskou as een van die mees geliefde gesange wat geskryf is gedurende die laaste deel van die 19de eeu. Die skryf van hierdie bedagsame en beeldskoon opgeboude teks is nog meer verstommend as ons in ag neem dat die skrywer byna heeltemal blind was en die skryf van hierdie gesang beskryf as die “vrug van baie geestelike lyding,” en “die vinnigste stukkie werk wat ek ooit in my lewe gedoen het.”

Gebore in Glasgow, Skotland, op 27 Maart 1842, het George Matheson as seun net gedeeltelike sig gehad, en nadat hy aan die Universiteit van Glasgow begin het, het sy sig vinnig aangehou agteruitgaan. Behalwe vir “oomblikke van skemeragtige sig,” was hy teen die ouderdom van 18 totaal blind. Hierdie belangrike beproewing van blindheid het na alle voorkoms ’n tragedie gelyk aangesien hy ’n ywerige en gretige geleerde was, maar dit het hom daartoe gelei om op die Here te vertrou, en dit het sy wandel met God versterk.

Hy het op die vroeë ouderdom van 15 in die universiteit begin en het in 1861 op 19-jarige ouderdom met hoë lof geëindig. Hy was ’n briljante geleerde en het selfs vier verdere jare ná die gradeplegtigheid in meer teologiese studies deurgebring, terwyl hy ongetroud gebly het. Na sy gradeplegtigheid het hy heeltemal afhanklik van ander geword, en baie op sy twee susters staatgemaak, wat so toegewy was dat hulle Latyn, Grieks en Hebreeus geleer het omdat hulle gedink het dit sou hom in sy teologiese studies kon help. Een van hulle het sy getroue mede-werker en helper deur sy lewe gebly en hom ondersteun in sy roeping as predikant en ander ampspligte.

Na voltooiing van sy teologiese kursus het hy assistentpredikant geword by die beroemde Dr. Macduff, in wie se kerk met duisende lede hy grootgemaak is. Binne kort is hy egter gekies as predikant van die Church of Scotland in die hawedorp en somerresort Innellan. Hier het hy agtien jaar gebly. Baie families het die somer daar deurgebring hoofsaaklik om deur sy prediking geïnspireer te word.

Wanneer hy gepreek het, het die oop Bybel voor hom op die kansel geleë gestaan, en vir die gemeente het dit gelyk asof hy daaruit lees. Gedurende die toesprake het sy oë reguit na die gemeente gekyk, en baie het weggegaan sonder ’n idee dat hulle net na ’n blinde prediker geluister het. Dit was gedurende hierdie tyd dat hy die gewoonte ontwikkel het om sy preke uit die hoof te leer, sowel as die Skrifafdelings wat hy in sy toesprake gebruik het. Sy geheue was so skerp dat as iemand een van sy voorbereide preke twee keer vir hom gelees het, of wat ook al hy wou memoriseer, hy dit van daardie punt af perfek kon herhaal. Op een Sondag egter, nadat hy dit vir 12 jaar so gedoen het, het sy geheue heeltemal in die middel van ’n kragtige preek ineenstort en het die onderwerp waarop hy gepreek het uit sy gedagtes verdwyn. Hy het gaan sit en ’n psalm aangevra om gesing te word, en ná die lied, met volmaakte kalmte aan die gehoor vertel wat gebeur het. Nadat dit gedoen was, het hy opgestaan, ’n nuwe teks uitgedeel en ’n geïmproviseerde preek van groot krag gelewer. Na daardie ervaring het George min van sy preke geskryf, en uiteindelik slegs ’n oorsig voorberei waarvan hy gepreek het.

Dr. Matheson se laaste amp as predikant het hy in 1886 op 44-jarige ouderdom aangeneem toe hy predikant geword het van die groot St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, waar sy welsprekende prediking konsekwent groot skares mense na die eredienste gelok het. Hier het hy 13 jaar gebly en sy kerk het van 1 494 lede tot 1 703 in die eerste vyf jaar gegroei. Hy het getrou die evangelie gebly predikend en het bekend geword as een van Skotland se uitstaande predikers en predikante en is hoog geag in Edinburgh waar hy gewoon het.

Daar is baie spekulasies gemaak oor die oorsaak van die geestelike nood wat die outeur aangespoor het om hierdie teks te skryf. ’n Baie gewilde verhaal, alhoewel nooit bevestig nie, is dat hierdie teks die gevolg was van die ernstige beproewing wat Matheson moes deurmaak nadat sy tulebruid hom net voor hul troue verlaat het toe sy van sy naderende totale blindheid verneem het. Al kan hierdie verhaal nie gedokumenteer word nie, is daar baie betekenisvolle aanduidings in hierdie gesang wat ’n bedroefde hart weerspieël, soos die “flikkerende toorts” en die “geleende straal” in die tweede vers, die nasporing van die “reënboog deur die reën” in die derde refrein, sowel as die “kruis” in die laaste vers.

Gelukkig het Dr. Matheson wel ’n rekening gegee van die skryf van hierdie gesang:

“My gesang is gecomponeer in die predikantswoning van Innellan op die aand van 6 Junie 1882. Ek was daardie tyd alleen. Dit was die dag van my suster se huwelik, en die res van die familie het oornag in Glasgow gebly. Iets het met my gebeur wat net vir myself bekend was, en wat my die ergste geestelike lyding veroorsaak het. Die gesang was die vrug van daardie lyding en was die vinnigste stukkie werk wat ek ooit in my lewe gedoen het. ’n Ware inspirasie — ek het eerder die indruk gehad dat dit vir my van ’n innerlike stem af gedikteer is as dat ek dit self uitgedink het. Ek is heel seker dat die hele werk in vyf minute voltooi is en ewe seker dat dit nooit deur my hande geretoucheer of gekorrigeer is nie. Ek het geen natuurlike gawe vir ritme nie. Al die ander verse wat ek ooit geskryf het is vervaardigde artikels; dit het soos ’n dagbreek van bo gekom. Ek het nooit weer daarin geslaag om dieselfde ywer in vers te herwin nie.”

Die gesang het eerste in die Church of Scotland se maandelikse tydskrif, Lewe en Werk, in Januarie 1883 verskyn. Die melodie is een jaar later deur ’n prominente Skotse orrelis van sy tyd, Albert L. Peace, gecomponeer, wat versoek is om ’n musiekstuk spesiaal vir Matheson se teks te skryf.

Peace se eie beskrywing van die skryf van hierdie fyn melodie is soos volg: “Ná dit sorgvuldig deur te lees, het ek die musiek reguit neergeskryf, en ek kan sê dat die ink van die eerste noot skaars droog was toe ek die melodie klaar gehad het.” Die oorsprong van of die naam van die melodie, St. Margaret, is onbekend behalwe dat dit ’n naam is wat in Skotland baie vereer word, en sekerlik ook vanweë die geliefde Koningin Margaret van Skotland.

Die later jare van Matheson se lewe van die ouderdom van 57 tot sy dood op 64 is bestee aan die skryf van sommige van die mooiste vroom skrifte in die Engelse taal, insluitend Moomente op die Berg, Stem van die Gees, en Rus by die Rivier. Alhoewel dit sy enigste gesang is wat in die meeste liedereboeke gevind word, het hy ’n paar ander uitstekende gesange geskryf, insluitende “Make Me A Captive Lord”, en “Then I Shall Be Free.”

Die vier sleutelwoorde van “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” is: liefde, lig, vreugde, en kruis. Hierdie woorde is beskryf as die volledige voldoening vir enige gelowige wie se lewe totaal oorgegee is aan die wil van God. Dit sou die res van iemand se lewe kan neem om die persoonlike betekenis van hierdie vier uitdrukkings ten volle te ontdek.

Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

Greetings of brotherly love to one and all. The year 2022 is almost gone. A lot has happened. Another year of devastating storms, floods, fires, earthquakes, wars, and rumors of wars. America has gone through another season of political elections, causing the conservatives and liberals to become even more polarized into opposing parties.

Recently, I have been reflecting on the current status of life as a committed Bible-believing Christian in our world today. Sure, there are certain places in our world where Christians live in constant threat of imprisonment or death simply because they are trying to live according to God’s Word. However, the world, seems to be moving towards an increasingly negative perspective of God’s people. In an increasingly developing trend, there is a surprising rise of hostility towards the committed believer.

What is happening? I have had numerous conversations with various believers from around the country who seem to have a growing alarm about the current victorious march of evil over good, of liberal agendas over a conservative lifestyle, and the list goes on. Current skyrocketing inflation, the potential of unprecedented heating costs for many, the rumors of rising interest rates, and the ongoing shortage of goods all tend to cause a person to be jolted out of a sense of normality.

For us as Christians, let us always keep our focus fixed on the God of heaven. This is the God that Paul declared on Mars Hill—God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; Neither is worshipped with men’s hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things; –Acts 17:24-25.

Let’s stop focusing on the fact that evil seems to be prevailing and increasing around us and then concluding that somehow Satan has the upper hand right now. Rather, let us be reminded about what God’s Word says. But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived. But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them; And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works –2 Timothy 3:13-17.

Let us keep our eyes fixed on Jesus …the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God –Hebrews 12:2. Instead of believing Satan’s lie that he is somehow winning the battle for Truth right now, let’s remember that the Bible reveals that Satan can do nothing without God allowing him a temporary free rein. It seemed to those looking on that Satan had the complete upper hand when Jesus was crucified and buried. Surprise, surprise! Satan had unwittingly allowed God to use him to accomplish everything that had been prophesied throughout the Scriptures. It is the same today… God will again allow Satan whatever free rein is necessary to bring to fulfillment all that the Bible has foretold will come to pass regarding the end of time.

In this issue of the magazine, we have once more endeavored to bring you information in the articles that is both helpful and relevant to our time in history. Brother Leonard Martin, a bishop in one of our churches has shared an exhortation on spiritual gifts in the church with a number of clear, practical observations for us today. The article that we have chosen to share from “Bible Helps” in this issue is one of the best discourses on the subject of “faith and works” that I have ever read. The writer even delves, with biblical simplicity and clarity, into the controversial subjects of divine election and predestination. Finally, we have The Foolishness of Preaching an evaluation regarding the basis of churches using “the altar call”—is it founded in the Scriptures and the history of the church or is it a method that the church has borrowed from the world in more recent years?!

All of this is sure to stir thoughts and discussion—which is our goal with these types of articles. Please feel free to respond via email or regular mail with your thoughts of caution or encouragement. This is helpful for us and our writers. When you write, we also ask that you mention yes or no if we can use your questions or comments in our magazine. We have had various requests to establish a section in our magazine dedicated to hearing from our readers.

One final thought… over the years our readers have, at times, shared with us ways that they think we could improve our magazine for the good of all who read it and to present a more clear gospel message. We welcome this to continue.

May God richly bless each of you,

Curvin L. Wenger
